MR. DEWAR  REFERENCE TO NEWSPAPER ARTICLE-ANNOUNCEMENT OF RESIGNATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of personal privilege which arises from a series of articles published in the Toronto Telegram on Wednesday, April 22, and subsequent dates.
I have known Harvey Lunam, proprietor of the Lunam Construction Company, for many years. In 1945, when I purchased a hotel, Harvey Lunam advanced me moneys which I repaid him in full in 1947, when I sold the hotel. Subsequently, I accommodated Harvey Lunam by exchanging cheques with him. That was one of his methods of financing when he was hard pressed for funds to meet his obligations. All those cheques were honoured by the banks on which they were drawn. I exchanged cheques with him over a period of nearly three years, from the middle of 1948 to the middle of 1951. He gave me cheques and I gave him covering cheques. I received no benefit and suffered no loss from these transactions. I did it to help an old friend.
The Lunam Construction Company, in response to public advertisements by the dominion government, tendered successfully and was awarded contracts to construct public works. In each case the company was the lowest bidder and met all of the conditions of the invitation to tender. I had no direct or indirect interest in the Lunam Construction Company, and have none now. I never profited from the Lunam Construction Company or from the public treasury.
This house will recall that I was elected in 1949. I did not believe that in continuing to help my friend Harvey Lunam I was violating the spirit of the law as it is applicable to members of the house. Fuller knowledge of parliamentary practices brought me to realize that the combination of circumstances might create false impressions, and I discontinued cheque exchanging.
It is worth mentioning that most of the buildings involved are not located in my constituency. It is also noteworthy that it
was almost one year after I stopped exchanging cheques with Harvey Lunam that following a serious automobile accident he failed to meet his obligations.
I deny any intentional wrongdoing and I repeat that I did not profit in any manner or fashion from my dealings with Harvey Lunam or the Lunam Construction Company.
I have enjoyed the friendship and camaraderie of my fellow members of the house. That I shall always prize.
I thank my constituents for the privilege of serving them, which I believe I did conscientiously and with credit. They were always uppermost in my thoughts and I spared no effort on their behalf.
We are now nearing dissolution. Consequently, I choose to place myself in the hands of my constituents. They will understand and have an opportunity to return me.
Regretfully, I tender my resignation as a member of the House of Commons.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the statement that has been made, I would ask the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) if it is his intention to inform the house now as to what steps he proposes to take to deal with the relationship of the Department of Public Works to this transaction which has just been discussed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MR. DEWAR  REFERENCE TO NEWSPAPER ARTICLE-ANNOUNCEMENT OF RESIGNATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Department of Public Works is competent to deal with the transaction between that department and the Lunam Construction Company and has been doing so. In view of statements that there are unpaid suppliers of materials and subcontractors, I am rather surprised that no proceedings have been instituted by those so-called creditors against their debtor. I understand that, when this Mr. Lunam met with this accident and ceased to carry on with the completion of his contracts, those
4510	HOUSE OF
Mr. A. E. Dewar-Resignation contracts were taken over by the department in conformity with the clause of the contract. I understand that there were several of those contracts, that with respect to some of them they will be completed and there will be from the contract price and the deposits a surplus available.
That situation presents a difficulty. It will not be up to the department to determine what will be the priorities with respect to claims on this surplus or what payments to creditors should be made. It would seem to me that this was an appropriate case for the placing of the affairs of this unfortunate contractor under the Bankruptcy Act where there would be a trustee who would take possession, who would receive all the claims and would then prepare, in the way provided by the act, a distribution of whatever is available in accordance with the priorities which prevail in the province of Saskatchewan and in accordance with the rules laid down in the act.
I have heard it said that it was intended to assert a claim for something beyond the contract price because of delays in supplying some of the equipment that had to be installed. That is something which a trustee would be quite competent to deal with. If there were grounds for such a claim and for submitting that claim, it would have to be considered. I am credibly informed that there were delays that had not been foreseen in procuring and supplying some of the equipment that had to be installed. It would not be the first time that that has happened, and it would not be the first time that that kind of a claim had to be dealt with. But it is generally stated and believed that this contracting firm is not capable of discharging its liabilities.
If that is the case, it is something which I think should be dealt with by the courts. The Bankruptcy Act contains all the provisions required to deal with that matter in a manner that would perhaps not satisfy all the creditors but which would treat all the creditors with equal justice and on the basis of the rules with respect to priorities recognized under the act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MR. DEWAR  REFERENCE TO NEWSPAPER ARTICLE-ANNOUNCEMENT OF RESIGNATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say
that the hon. gentleman is much better informed than I am. This is the first time I have heard the suggestion made that this contracting firm had failed to complete contracts in 1948 and had involved the Great-West Life Assurance Company in any way whatsoever.
The contracts that are let by the government have to be let in a manner provided by the statutes adopted by this parliament; and the government is always subject to severe criticism-and rightly so-if the low tenderer who complies with the conditions for tendering is not awarded the contract. When it is felt that it would be imprudent to award a contract to the low tenderer, the matter is brought before council; and I can assure the hon. gentleman that when it is brought before council there must be extremely serious grounds to induce the members of council to depart from the principle that a low tenderer who has complied with the conditions and who has made the required deposit should be awarded the contract.
It does happen. Not long ago there was a tender that was lower than the one of the tenderer to whom the contract was awarded; but the invitation for tenders contained the stipulation that the tenderer would have to satisfy the department that he had had previous experience in similar undertakings. This was a company that was just entering the field in Canada, composed of gentlemen who claimed that they had had experience in similar work in other countries, but they had no experience in similar work in this country. We finally came to the conclusion that they did not comply with the requirements, they did not satisfy the department that they had the required experience. But this requirement that the contracts be awarded to the low tenderer is on the whole a wise one, and that the low tender on all these jobs can be disregarded only when there are good grounds for doing so, the sufficiency of which the government has to take the responsibility of justifying to this house.

I am unaware that there had been any indication before this that the Lunam contracting firm was not a firm that should be considered when its tender happened to be the lowest, and it had complied with the other conditions of the invitation to submit tenders.

There are a number of questions on the order paper at this time that indicate the nature of the inquiries which should be pursued, and I suggest that that would be the proper way in which to deal with this subject.

speechtext:

Inquiries of the Ministry me prior notice of his question. The particular news item to which he has referred has been brought to my attention. I have no comment to make, other than that the news item is just speculation-probably an educated guess.

maintopic: SUBVENTION ON PRODUCTION IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: What do you mean by that?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: SUBVENTION ON PRODUCTION IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
The railways since 1938 have been paid a transportation subvention to the extent of 5 mills per ton mile with a maximum of $3 a ton, for Canadian coal used on company service, to make such coal competitive with American coal at the same coaling points.
The Canadian National Railways, in recent years, has claimed that this 5 mills per ton mile is not a true assessment of their costs. At present a study is being made of the Canadian National Railways' costs by an independent commissioner, under the direction of the dominion coal board and the Department of Transport. Until that investigation is completed, the Canadian National Railways is continuing to buy coal in the same quantities as last year, and the dominion coal board is assisting in order to give the maximum tonnage available to all operators affected.
At the present time the government does not intend to increase subventions either for the railways or for the movement of domestic and industrial coal, unless this investigation should show that the railways are not being adequately paid.

I have received a copy of the Crown News, which is distributed throughout the first commonwealth division. The issue I have is that of Friday, November 28, 1952. This publication contains news from different parts of the commonwealth and under the heading "By our Maple Leaf Reporter" I find the following:
Votes of "no confidence" in federal parliament.
The leaders of the socialist and C.C.F. parties, Mr. Coldwell and Mr. Drew, both put down motions of no confidence in the government on Wednesday. The socialist leader said that in its failure to begin a national health scheme, the government had not fulfilled its pledge to the people. Mr. Drew attacked the government on the grounds of wasteful defence expenditure. Government extravagance, he said, was the cause of the very heavy taxation the people had to bear.
I do not question the accuracy of the last part of that statement. While I take no offence in regard to any inaccuracies in this, I do believe that perhaps we might expect that news communications which are distributed among our troops in Korea and which purport to be on the basis of reliable reports from the different nations in the commonwealth might bear a little more relationship

to the actual political divisions within this house and throughout the country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: As the hon. member for Melfort knows, as the railway is wholly government owned it cannot spend anything without government approval. That is why these items come before parliament. The budget is approved by the parliamentary committee on railways and shipping. If there is a deficit, the deficit has to be voted by parliament. In so far as branch lines are concerned, they go forward after a recommendation comes to the government from the board of directors of the railroad. Then the government must decide whether or not it is prepared to support the recommendation. Extensions of recent years that can be recalled are the Barraute line, the Kitimat line and the Lynn Lake line. I asked him if it would be possible for some of these changes, when they were brought in, to be made retroactive to the date that would have been the effective date had the bill been brought in in 1952.
As the minister knows, he answered in the first place by saying it would not be possible to do that. The answer is recorded
[Mr. Abbott.l

It is possible that some of the changed provisions of the Civil Service Superannuation Act could be made retroactive, but I think it is unlikely that all of them could be.
When I asked the question I imagine the minister knew on that occasion what was in my mind. I had in mind the situation that would develop with respect to people who would retire between that date and the time when the new legislation would come into effect. It would not have been possible to get it in at any reasonable time during last year's session because the amount of work that has been involved in the revision of this act has been tremendous. After reviewing the situation this year when we finally determined the measure we would recommend, we came to the conclusion it would be neither practicable nor desirable to make the effective date go back beyond January 1, 1953. One must always have a cut-off date in matters of this kind. In view of the fact that this measure was being introduced in March or April, 1953, the appropriate date to make it effective seemed to be January 1, 1953, and that decision was taken.

I should like to make a comment on that matter. I am glad the minister has made this statement, because, as he said, we found ourselves in real difficulty. There was a strong feeling that certain special groups-not large in numbers, and notably some of the officials of the old department of soldiers' civil re-establishment-were suffering from what looked like an inequity. The situation at that time was rather amusing in its way. It seemed as though some of the departments carried on in splendid isolation and without much cooperation. I think it is not an exaggeration to say that the department of soldiers' civil reestablishment at that time sought virtually to run a pension scheme of its own and had sent money from time to time to the Department of Finance, hoping thereby to give this scheme an over-all validity. Their subscriptions were month by month regularly returned. The result was that certain of the employees who, in good faith, had made their pension subscriptions-which were eventually returned to them-for some years felt that they had a status which later on it was suggested they did not have.
The equity of the situation was fully appreciated by the minister's officials and, I think I may say, by the parliamentary assistant who was there. I am glad that the minister has made this statement which, as I understand it, will mean that the situation can be looked into and every effort can be made to bring about equity. The numbers involved are only a few score, so that the actual amount involved is not large.
My recollection also is that it was pointed out that this bill, which we all welcome because it is a great step forward in the relationship with the civil service, nevertheless involves a good deal of constructive work and has a good many new features. I think there was a feeling that it is not like the laws of the Medes and the Persians that can never be changed. As time goes on and this inquiry which the minister, I am glad to say, has referred to, is made, it will be possible to review the situation if equity seems to demand it.
I might just add also-and this refers to one part of the minister's statement-that it was extraordinarily difficult to feel that we had obtained all the facts. There were one or two members of the committee who had made a special study of the facts over the years; but at the end of our deliberations I


think even they felt they were not sure that we had got the last bit of detail affecting those classes. I am glad therefore of the statement the minister has made.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION OF PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS

Perhaps I could take a moment of the committee's time to place on record one thing which I think should be said, namely, a word of appreciation for the complete unanimity of opinion, as to the general equity and virtue of this bill, that was shown in the committee's study of it. I am very grateful for that fact. All members in the House of Commons serving on the committee seemed to be completely together in their view as to what should be done. There was one outstanding problem with respect to a relatively small group, and I am delighted with the statement of the minister today. I think that is the best way of dealing with the matter. We got to a stage in the committee where we were not sure of the facts, and it would seem as if the associations and others just did not have all the facts relative to the problem. I refer of course to those employees in the old department of soldiers' civil re-establishment and a small group in the interior department. This assurance of the minister that there will be a detailed examination of the facts in these cases will provide the right way of remedying any injustices that may have been committed.
I also note the statement that if there are substantial injustices in principle not remedied the minister will see that consideration is given to the method of correcting them as well. I think that is a better method than attempting an amendment to the bill at this stage on the information or the lack of information concerning the group who felt that they had an injustice.

I am sure we all welcome
the statement the Minister of Finance has just made. It often happens in our experience here that when a new piece of legislation is put on the statute books, that is it; we have had it for some time. I am very glad to note the attitude of the Minister of Finance this morning, and also his statement that where there seem to be injustices any steps necessary to correct any injustices that the minister feels should be corrected will be taken. I take it from that that if it should happen that an amendment is necessary to this new act to take care of injustices that the minister is satisfied should be corrected the necessary amendment will be brought in at the next session of parliament, if the minister is still in charge of the finance department.

In other words, generally speaking, I think it is appropriate for us to say from the opposition side of the house that this is pretty good legislation; we may find some shortcomings in it, but nevertheless we welcome it and we are glad to give it our support.
While we are on clause 1 of the bill I should like to ask the minister whether any further consideration has been given by him since the debates in the house on the resolution stage and on second reading to the problem of retired civil servants on low pensions. As he recalls, that matter was referred to by several of those who took part in that debate, and the support for doing something for these people seemed to be quite strong. It is not out of place for me to say to the minister that after that debate was over I received word that a change had just been made in Manitoba, and I took occasion to speak to him one day out in the hall and to call it to his attention.
In other words Manitoba must now be added to the list of those jurisdictions that have done something for their retired civil servants. Those that I now know of are the United States, the United Kingdom, Newfoundland, Saskatchewan and Manitoba.
I also point out that the Canadian Pacific Railway-although the provision made is very small-has done something for its retired employees who were on low pensions, provided they are not yet 70 years of age. In the case of Manitoba the provision made at this year's session of the legislature was for civil servants between the age of retirement and the age of seventy. The increase of their pension amounts to 25 per cent, pro-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PROVISION OF PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
My memory is that I gave it the other day, perhaps in answer to a question of my hon. friend. Speaking from memory, I think the actuarial deficit of the fund is now approximately $189 million Again speaking from memory, I think this

Public Service Superannuation Act house voted $75 million in two successive years and $25 million this year; and after making these appropriations and after adopting the new basis of protecting the fund by matching the contributions of employees for both current and prior service, of paying interest on the actuarial deficits, as well as on the amount actually in the fund, the approximate actuarial deficit today is $189 million. I have indicated on previous occasions that I felt that as and when circumstances were appropriate this house should vote additional sums to fill that hole.
I have never felt that it would be quite appropriate to put new taxes on in order to do that in any particular length of time, but I think we should continually bear in mind that that deficit exists and that it should be filled and that the present bill again provides actuarial reports every five years. So parliament will be constantly informed of the position of the fund from time to time.
Before I take my seat I should like to express appreciation of what has been said this morning about the general nature of the bill. I share the views of hon. members. I do that in any particular length of time, but I think we should continually bear in mind that that deficit exists and that it should be filled and that the present bill again provides actuarial reports every five years. So parliament will be constantly informed of the position of the fund from time to time.
As I said in the debate on second reading, credit must also go to the advisory committee composed of civil servants in other departments of government, who have given a great deal of their time and knowledge to the development of this piece of legislation.
Referring for a moment to what was said by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, let me say that I never consider a piece of legislation as being in the nature of the laws of the Medes and Persians. It is always susceptible of improvement. This represents a major step forward. But if next year it is found that some provisions have been overlooked and some improvements could be made then, whoever is the minister responsible for introducing the measure would be only too happy I am sure to make them.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as a member of the committee I wish to say only a word. I believe there is general approval of the measure among civil servants and among the people of Canada generally. It affects 60,000 people and, naturally, they are particularly interested.

One important point is that it clarifies the situation in regard to long-term temporary employees in the civil service. I was sorry I could not be in the chamber when the minister made his statement, but I understood pretty well what it would be. I understand he is carrying forward certain studies in connection with certain persons many of us think should have received special consideration.
I had hoped personally that this would be done this year, because these people have been waiting for a long time to have what they considered a wrong corrected. During the debate at the resolution stage I pointed out that the matter affecting the old department of soldiers' civil re-establishment had been up before the veterans committee on a number of occasions, and that the Canadian Legion had made representations to the government. They had also requested that the matter be given consideration by the veterans affairs committee. However, under the terms of reference of our committee we were not permitted to include a discussion of that matter.
I felt so strongly about it that in committee I moved an amendment, which I believe would make the necessary correction, in which I recommended that the government consider giving further assistance to the personnel of the department of soldiers' civil re-establishment. The amendment was received favourably in principle, but it was thought that it was broader than it should be. I withdrew it on that account, with the assurance from the chairman of the committee that quite probably further consideration would be given. In any event we were assured the minister would be consulted; and it was felt that he would give sympathetic consideration to the matter. As I say, I am pleased now that this has been done.
On different occasions the veterans have asked consideration of the 12 per cent feature -the payment of their own contribution and that of the government when war service was included. This matter did not receive much consideration in committee, and I have nothing more to say about it this morning. It is a matter about which many veterans feel strongly. The fact that comparatively few took advantage of the opportunity granted them of paying the double amount indicates that they do not consider it a very generous offer.
Another provision set out in the act is that changing the date for the close of world war I. I recall that on numerous occasions veterans have requested that this be done, and I am pleased that it has been done.
I do not think it is necessary to repeat the arguments presented in connection with those B8108-286
23, 1353
Public Service Superannuation Act who were connected with the department of soldiers' re-establishment and also the small group of civil servants in the old interior department. These people had served since the end of the first war. I know many of them personally and, as all hon. members are aware, they have given excellent service. We and they considered that it was only because of a technicality that they had not been included in the permanent service. Some 500 of them after 1924 contributed to the fund on the assumption and with the feeling that they were entitled to be considered as permanent. We understand that the moneys they contributed were not accepted by the civil service branch. Those funds were held until 1927 and then returned to them. I feel strongly that these persons should be included. While I regret an amendment was not made to the act to include them at this time, I appreciate the fact that the minister is going to consider the matter, and I would hope he might consider it favourably.
I should like to quote P.C. 3560 of October 3, 1921, which indicates quite clearly that these people were considered by the authorities at that time as being permanent. This reads:
And whereas the staff of the board of pension commissioners of Canada has recently been amalgamated with the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment under the direction of the latter and the work of the combined organizations is now approaching a permanent basis;
It was considered in 1921, shortly after the war, that they were on a permanent basis. It is now 1953 and they have not been accepted as being on a permanent basis. The order in council continues:
And whereas the soldier settlement board has now reached a stage where the general business of the board, including the collection of moneys loaned, will continue for some years to come and may be regarded as on a permanent basis.
When the soldier settlement board was set up after the war I think it was considered that it would be temporary in nature and that possibly after a few years it could be done away with. It is a long time from 1919 to 1953. Permanent civil servants were taken in by other departments to do exactly the same work as these men and were considered as permanent civil servants while these men were not. I am not going to labour the point any further. I am pleased that the matter is going to receive further consideration and I trust that the position of these men will be looked into.

It is my opinion that this whole question should be thoroughly investigated to establish the facts. I think we should be absolutely clear as to the facts in these cases because this is a highly technical measure. If we are not careful to handle it properly there may be the possibility of charges of real discrimination by those who feel that they should be given comparable treatment. , Mr. Knowles: I wonder if the committee gave any consideration to one aspect of the provision that accords to civil servants the right to elect to cover prior service. It was felt that, in such circumstances, if he finally decides at some later date that it is in his interest to do so he should not be able -if I may use the colloquial phrase-to bet against the actuarial position of the fund by waiting until some future time to make such a decision. Mr. Speaker, just before third reading is given, there is a brief word I should like to say. In his reply the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) said that comparisons as to what is done for retired civil servants should not be made with other governments without at the same time comparing the beneficial provisions of this legislation. I do not wish to detract by one iota from the praise that the minister feels is coming to this superannuation act so far as its provisions at the present time are concerned. It is good legislation and it will stand up favourably alongside that of any other government or jurisdiction. But when we enter our plea, as we do, on behalf of retired civil servants whose pensions are in the lower brackets, I ask the minister to remember that many of these people were retired when the provisions of this legislation were not so generous and were not so beneficial as they are at the present time. He said a moment ago that when I raised this matter this morning it was a case of raising it again; he could say "again and again". He knows that some of us will continue to do so, for we feel that these people really have consideration coming to them.
From what has been said today, it appears that the present Minister of Finance has closed the door to the possibility of anything being done for these people within the confines of the Public Service Superannuation Act. However, although he closed that door, he left another door open, namely the possibility of something being done for these people by way of a special vote in the estimates. At least we now know what to ask for in precise terms. I feel strongly that our retired civil servants, particularly those in the lower brackets, have an increase coming to them to meet the increase in the cost of living. This principle has been recognized by the governments of the United States, the United Kingdom, Newfoundland, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. I therefore feel that something should be done here. We shall continue to press the matter, and I hope it will not be long until, to use the minister's

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I propose to deal with a suggestion which I made earlier today and which was not accepted at that time. I proposed that a select committee of members of this house be appointed to examine into the circumstances under which contracts were awarded to the Lunam Construction Company and the nature of the supervision exercised in a case of that kind. I am dealing now entirely with the responsibility of the government in relation to the awarding of contracts of this nature, and the inescapable fact that those who deal with a contractor, as subcontractors or otherwise, have reason to believe that they are engaged in a safe type of employment and that they do in fact have a measure of protection that is appropriate in relation to contracts awarded by the government.
I am also bearing in mind the fact that in the handling of public contracts, the extent of the supervision that is exercised is, in itself, the one assurance that we have as members of parliament or that the people of Canada generally can have that there is in the handling of public funds that care which will prevent waste, extravagance and unsupervised spending, all of which in the end amounts to a burden upon the taxpayer of the country.
When I raised this subject this morning it was explained that the contracts in question had been let by tender, and that emphasis has been placed in this house upon the desirability of respecting the tender system. I subscribed to that statement. In fact I have had occasion to raise some question about certain contracts that were let without tender. Nevertheless there is something more than the tender itself. There is the question of the ability of any contractor to carry out the contract. There is also the fact that accumulating obligations are of concern not only to the people to whom debts may be owed, but also to the government which has undertaken certain public

construction on behalf of the people of Canada, and must at all times be concerned with the manner in which that is carried out, and also the relationship that exists between the government and those who are performing work of that kind.
We all recognize that the circumstances under which work is carried out have a large bearing on the efficiency of the undertaking and the ultimate cost. I refer to a discussion which took place in general terms on April 8 last, as reported at page 3617 of Hansard. I merely wish to refer to the quotations appearing on that page which I shall read. After some discussion of the way in which these contracts had been awarded, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier), in referring to the Lunam Construction Company, used these words:
They were competent tenderers.
Very shortly afterwards he said:
We sign a contract with the lowest tenderer. He proceeds with the work. Our officials in the field make progress reports.
It has been amply demonstrated, Mr. Speaker, that the Lunam Construction Company were not competent tenderers, whatever else they may have been. They were not able to carry out the undertaking, and while we have not yet those figures before us, I find that the Toronto Telegram of Saturday, April 25, 1953, reports an interview with the Minister of Public Works in which the interview is summed up in these words in the headline: "Let Lunam pay;" and then the subheading is: "Government washes its hands of $239,000 left unpaid on Lunam subcontracts." I have read the report and it would seem that the heading and subheading to which I have referred represent an accurate condensation of that report. If that is the exact figure, it is a large sum of money for which there is apparently little now to pay those who worked on those contracts.
Some question was raised this morning as to why bankruptcy proceedings had not been taken. I have no thought of venturing any guess in that respect. We all know of course that sometimes bankruptcy proceedings are not taken if the assets are likely to be so little that no one is ready to assume the personal expenses involved in the proceedings which might produce very little in the way of financial results. We do know that some payments have been made, if the reports on this subject have been correct, payments in relatively small sums.
The point I wish to make, however, is that these contracts were let under circumstances which suggested reasons for caution and for some examination as to the ability of this contractor to complete the contracts. After
29, 1953
Lunam Construction Company all, the government had decided it was important that these various projects be completed. Since the government was acting on behalf of the people it was important that the government be sure they could be completed; it was important that the supervision of the expenditure be constant and adequate; it was important also that those who had some reason to look to a government contract as offering a substantial measure of security in that very fact would not find themselves in the position in which they find themselves on this occasion.
During the present session we have had a good deal of discussion about the desirability of bringing all the business of parliament back under the control of parliament. On this side we have objected strenuously to the re-enactment of the Emergency Powers Act which had the effect of making it possible for the government to carry on a great part of the business of this country, if they chose to do so, without obtaining direct authority from parliament in regard to that. But in that case, having regard to the existence of legislation of that kind, having regard to the heavy expenditures on construction of all kinds, having regard to the vital necessity of economy wherever economy could be practised so that we protect the taxpayers of this country against overtaxation which is the result of extravagance and waste, I believe it is the duty of parliament to insist that it know what takes place.
We understand that this parliament will shortly terminate its activities. All the more reason that we should know what did take place in this case so that the authority of parliament may be exercised to establish some effective measure of supervision over contracts of this kind. This may be only one contract in itself. If there is no greater assurance that other contracts are to be supervised effectively than is furnished by this case, then I submit that hon. members have a right, yes, and I believe a duty, to insist that they know what actually did take place; that they know what procedure is followed in dealing with contracts of this kind; and that they be able, as a result of that information, to establish a more effective system in the future.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker):
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this house a select committee should be appointed immediately to inqure into the circumstances under which contracts were awarded by the government to the Lunam Construction Company, the steps that were taken to supervise the completion of the said contracts, and the failure of the government to take appropriate steps to protect subcontractors and others in regard to
4530	HOUSE OF
Lunam Construction Company payment for work performed and materials supplied under these contracts."

Mr. Speaker, in view of the statements which have just been made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), and the circumstances under which this matter is being discussed today, I feel we must support the amendment to the motion to go into supply.
I may say that I have been very unhappy about this matter ever since it was first raised in the house some days ago by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). I lived in Regina for a number of years, and I have some knowledge of Mr. Lunam's background; and it seems difficult for me, in view of the stories in Regina in the middle thirties, to understand why Mr. Lunam was regarded as a competent tenderer for government contracts. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was in Regina, too, at the same time; and I do not know whether his view of Mr. Lunam's activities at that time is the same as mine. However, I find it difficult to understand how he could be regarded as a competent contractor.
However, be that as it may, I think the house would be justified in making an inquiry. Indeed, I am going to support the proposal of the Leader of the Opposition for a select committee. I think perhaps if I had been making the proposal I might have suggested a judicial inquiry. However, the one suggested should meet the needs of the situation at the present time.
I think there should be an inquiry into the circumstances, and I hope that such committee will make constructive suggestions when it reports. After all, the matter that has been before the house today is one which, so far as a personality is concerned, is ended. But the matter of the circumstances connected with the contracts, and the method of the letting of these contracts, are matters which concern the whole house.
I am not criticizing the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier). I fully realize that a minister dealing with a department of this size, and with a large number of contracts in varying amounts, cannot know about every contract or every detail in those contracts. Nevertheless I think we have to be safeguarded, and that future ministers have to be safeguarded against the kind of thing with which we have been faced in the house in the last week or two in this connection.
And so, Mr. Speaker, I am going to support the motion, because I believe it is fully warranted at the present time. I would hope that perhaps even the government might accept the suggestion for an inquiry.

Mr. Speaker, I feel I should support the amendment that has been moved by the Leader of the Opposition, because I think it is in the best interests of the country, of the House of Commons and even of the government itself that an inquiry be made into the subjects named in this amendment.
I want the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) to know that in supporting the amendment I do not mean to cast any reflection upon him. I do believe that the people of the country feel that it is our duty and responsibility to get as much information as we can in this whole matter, so that proper safeguards can be set up against this sort of thing happening in the future. So I propose to support the amendment. I hope the government will look with favour upon it.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in spite of the hopes of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), if they will only look at the amendment they will realize at once that it is quite impossible for the government to accept it. It is clearly a motion of no confidence, condemning the government for having failed to take appropriate steps to protect subcontractors and others in regard to payment for work performed and materials supplied under these contracts.
Now, it may be the hope of hon. members that there will be a majority in the House of Commons prepared to express that censure of no confidence in the government. But to ask the government itself to repudiate itself is something which we simply cannot do, especially when it has been explained that these contracts were let in the usual way, and that they were granted to the lowest tenderer who had complied with the conditions set out in the notice calling for tenders*
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar says that in the thirties he was residing in Regina, and that something happened at that time which would have made him dubious about the propriety of giving a substantial contract to the Lunam Construction Company. That is something which certainly does not appear in the government files, and certainly something which was entirely unknown to the officials of the department who received, checked, reported upon and recommended the granting of the contract to the lowest tenderer who had complied with the conditions upon which tenders were called.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) spoke this morning about something which happened in 1948, and which involved the Great-West Life Assurance Company, and

stated that the fact that the Great-West Life Assurance Company was involved would indicate sufficiently where this did take place. Well, to me it does not indicate where this did take place; because it is my knowledge that the Great-West Life Assurance Company operates throughout the whole of Canada and I think, also, beyond the boundaries of Canada. It is one of our largest assurance companies, and is represented in the important centres of the various provinces of Canada. I think it is also represented abroad.
That is something which was entirely unknown to the department or to the government; and perhaps this will be taken as an indication that there should be more care taken in ascertaining the competence of contractors, even when they are the low tenderers. I know it does happen sometimes that the very amount of a tender is a notice that it might be imprudent to accept it. And it is quite possible that some of the difficulties of this contractor may lie in the fact that his estimate was below the estimate that was made by others who tendered on the contract. Sometimes there are substantial discrepancies. I am told that in these cases the differences between the low tenderer and the next low tenderer varied from 4 per cent to 10 per cent. That is not unusual. That margin obviously does not indicate that the low tenderer is altogether out of line. Variations of from 4 to 10 per cent are not infrequent in tenders submitted by contractors.
Now, the contracts were let and they proceeded satisfactorily until the time when this contractor met with an automobile accident which put him in the hospital for several weeks. It was during that period that the difficulties became apparent. I am not suggesting that they did not exist before. There was an exchange of cheques to take an unfair advantage of the bankers. There may not be any law against the exchange of cheques in that way and thus taking that kind of advantage of our banking practices, but it is certainly an abuse. If one has to resort to that it does indicate that his situation is not the kind of situation that inspires confidence. But that was something which was not in the knowledge of the government or of the officials of the Department of Public Works.
As to the suggestion that there were no proceedings instituted to investigate the affairs of a man who was not paying his obligations as a result of the fact that there were no obvious assets that would even cover the expenses involved, I am told that there are several thousand dollars here that are going to be available. The hon. gentleman mentioned that there was $3,000.
29, 1953
Lunam Construction Company
$3,500 is what the minister said on April 8.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Even about that I am sure we will want to take another view. It is likely now that this debtor has not sufficient assets to satisfy all his creditors. I do not think it would be proper for the crown to take a surplus arising under one contract and apply it against a deficit under another contract. That would be getting an unfair portion of the available assets. If there are not sufficient assets to satisfy all obligations I think the crown should rank along with the other creditors and would not be justified in applying a surplus arising out of one contract to a debt arising out of another, though it may be the same contractor and the crown in both instances.
I think that we will have to take the view that, if there are insufficient assets to cover the liabilities, the liabilities under such contracts as cannot be completed for the amount available under each of them should be a claim that would rank with the claims of other creditors and should not be enforced in such a way as to provide preferential payment to the crown.
I think it was the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) who said that there appeared to be $170,000 of claims unsatisfied for materials and supplies. That would seem to indicate that there was work performed and there were materials supplied when the progress estimates came to the department and called for certain payments. I am informed that it was only after this accident to the contractor and after he got into the hospital that there was any notification from suppliers or subcontractors that they had claims outstanding. This is something which was handled in the ordinary way and the government cannot admit that it has failed in anything it was required to do in connection with these contracts.

Mr. Speaker, the very judicial manner in which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) dealt with this matter will be followed by myself who first brought the matter to the attention of parliament. All of us will feel that this has been an agonizing day for parliament, possibly a day of disenchantment. It is in the spirit, however, of realizing that on occasions like this parliament must rise above narrow partisanship that I am going to speak on this occasion. The Prime Minister dealt with this matter in a way that, while I cannot agree with his conclusions, nonetheless I will follow. I shall deal with the various matters in the order in which they arose in the house and also with the answers given
4532	HOUSE OF
Lunam Construction Company by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) when the matter was first discussed in the house.
The first answers to questions that were asked appear on pages 1308 and 1309 of Hansard of January 26. I had asked for details of the contracts that this company had. I disagree immediately when the Prime Minister says that this was a company of financial repute. It had no assets and it has no assets now. It had all the appearances of what I referred to on one occasion as a fly-by-night company without any visible capital. Yet it received a large number of government contracts. Naturally it was able to carry on and do that which the Prime Minister has just referred to, secure supplies from subcontractors to the extent of what I believed was $170,000 when I spoke in April but which as a result of examinations made by Judith Robinson has been found to be $230,000.
The figure of $170,000 was one I secured as a result of questions asked in parliament. Apparently the figures that were before the Department of Public Works were insufficient in amount and did not represent the true story of this debacle, one of the most serious I believe that has occurred in a long while. The facts would never have been found out through the questions asked in parliament had it not been that Miss Robinson apparently found it interesting on the facts revealed to make an examination which resulted in the finding out of things that parliament would never have found out.
On February 11 I asked further questions in the house as reported on page 1828 of Hansard. I am not going into the particulars of this question. But there are even yet a number of questions upon which parliament has not been vouchsafed any information. On March 11 the following motion for papers was passed by the house:
For a copy of all correspondence and telegrams since the first day of January, 1951 between any department of government and the Lunam Construction Company Limited of Regina, Saskatchewan, having to do with the failure of the said company to complete its several contracts, and in particular referring to the work progress reports submitted by it on the various construction projects under consideration by the same company, together with any statements on file containing the liabilities of the said company.
That was on March 11. That is information that parliament needs, but apparently that request for information has not aroused the interest of the department to the extent that one would have expected on a matter as important as this. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has said that payments made by the Department of Public Works were made on the basis of progress reports.


Progress reports, in order to be effectual, require first an affidavit or declaration of the contractor, as the case may be, and in addition they require certificates on the part of suppliers or subcontractors setting out that they in fact have received payment for the amounts which the contractor in turn is asking the department to pay. None of these answers have been given. There has been no reply to that important question. Replies should have taken no very great length of time; for, if progress reports are on file, it should not take long to produce copies.
In addition, other questions were asked. On the 25th of March the following question was asked:
1.	How many building or repair contracts have been granted to the Lunam Construction Company of Saskatchewan or the Lunam Construction Company Limited, in all departments of government other than public works, since the first of January, 1948?
2.	What were the contract prices of each of the said contracts and how much has been paid on account of each of them to the said company?
3.	Was work on one or more of said contracts discontinued by the said company before completion, and if so, in respect to which contracts?
4.	What did it cost to complete the contracts which were uncompleted by the said company?
5.	Were any materials or services unpaid by the said company?
6.	If so, what is the total amount of such materials or services on which any of the departments have notice or information?
That was on March 25, over one month ago, and as yet there is no answer. That indicates one of two things, either that the government does not want to reply or that the accounting system in the department is of such a nature that these particular documents are not available. On the one hand it is a case of dilatory action for the purpose of keeping parliament uninformed, or on the other hand it is an indictment of the government for its failure to have in effect the type of accounting system that would render such information instantly available, particularly when the last work done in respect of which this information is sought was over a year and two months ago.
The Prime Minister took the stand a moment ago, as he did this morning, that after all bankruptcy proceedings could be taken. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) covered that point in a few words. In so far as the liabilities of this company are concerned, and work that has been done for public works and Indian affairs but which is unpaid, we know that the suppliers and the workmen have $240,000 coming to them, and the only asset that is visible is the asset referred to by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) when he said that when all the contracts were completed there would be

a surplus of $3,500 to the credit of this company. If there were no costs in connection with bankruptcy proceedings and if trust companies accepted such work without compensation, then on the basis of my computation it would mean that the creditors, the suppliers and workmen who are still owed money would receive one and a half cents on the dollar.
When the matter was first brought to the attention of the Department of Public Works in 1952, the first answer given to those who were applying for payment was that some of the contractors had made false statements, that they had signed false progress reports.

speechtext: Did my department give that answer?
No; that is information we got outside of parliament and which we could not get here.
Oh, oh.
Hearsay.

I am making this statement as to what took place. When the minister says, "Did we give you that answer?", my reply immediately is no. Replies to our questions which would have indicated the situation have so far been denied to parliament, either intentionally or accidentally.
Cheap stuff.
Several contractors were advised that the reason for the delay was that they themselves were to blame in that they had given false reports of the progress of the work.

speechtext: Would my hon. friend mind saying by whom they were advised?

By the departmental
officials in Regina.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Can the hon. gentleman name them?

I am naming them as departmental officials. When it was found that there was only one in that position, the next thing that happened was that it was stated that because of Mr. Lunam's accident things had got behind. It was not Mr. Lunam's accident that put things behind. Mr. Lunam's accident but intensified and accelerated the situation. In other words, at the time of his injury he in fact was unable to pay the subcontractors. He in fact had accepted payments from the department under false declarations.
I shall refer to the false declarations in a moment. But the one thing that it is difficult 68108-2871
Lunam Construction Company for many of these people who have been defrauded to understand is the fact that payment has been denied to several of them who continued to supply materials in great volume for two months after Lunam's accident, and for two months after the government had discontinued its relationship with him and was looking for other contractors. Certainly there can be no excuse for denying payment to those contractors who, after Mr. Lunam's accident, continued to supply materials believing that they would be protected as people dealing with governments as subcontractors always are. There was not a word from anyone on the inspection staff of the Department of Public Works. Remember that Lunam no longer has any interest. My information is that in one case the subcontractor tried to remove several hundred dollars' worth of stuff which had been delivered after the Department of Public Works had cancelled its relationship, and the subcontractor was denied that opportunity.
When I brought this matter up, I brought it up because I believed that parliament would accept it as a principle that it would place itself in no higher position than the private contractor. As against the private contractor, however, the subcontractor and the workman have the right of a mechanic's lien. They can protect themselves if they are dealing with a company that is of the fly-by-night type. If perchance they were dealing with a company whose only capital was political fitness, then at least they would know and would have filed mechanics' liens to protect themselves. No such opportunity comes to the person who subcontracts under government.
I brought the matter to the attention of the Minister of Public Works on April 8. We dealt with the matter at some length in the house and the minister said, in effect, that it was difficult to find the whereabouts of Mr. Lunam; that he was a disappearing phantom who, having accumulated $240,000 worth of liabilities, vanished and could not be found. At the time I asked the question: How is it that the Regina Leader-Post reporters can find him? No answer came. They have been trying to find him since February, 1952. I asked a question, to which a reply was given today, and I find there is no correspondence between the Department of Public Works and any government official in Saskatchewan, the purpose of which has been to locate the whereabouts of the allegedly unlocatable. Yet Lunam has been in Regina week after week since February, 1952. The contractors and the workers have been asking for consideration from the government. They
4534	HOUSE OF
Lunam Construction Company have been met by delay; they have been met by everything but action.
Now, sir, these are a few circumstances that I think deserve consideration. Why should the government or Her Majesty be in a position where tradesmen trust governments and government representatives, where tradesmen knowing that there was a contract should be placed on their guard as to whether or not they should advance credit to a company with a contract with Her Majesty? Provision is made in the contract for progress reports. Under the contract the contractor agrees to pay the subcontractors. Either that means what it says, Mr. Speaker, that the contractor will not be paid before the Department of Public Works is satisfied that the contractor has settled with the subcontractor, or it means nothing. No bond, such as is ordinarily required, is required by the government, and the reason for it, as I understand from looking at the record, is that it would be a most costly thing to provide for bonds. The government, in fact, becomes its own bondsman. Many companies do not have insurance in certain particulars. They carry their own. They find it cheaper. When the practice of having bonds was first discontinued, the reason given was that it would be cheaper for the government of Canada to carry its own instead of paying insurance.
I point out these circumstances. I point out the failure of the government to notify those tradesmen who honestly continued, after February, 1952, and after the accident to Mr. Lunam, to supply goods, merchandise, wares and labour.
Then I come to the next thing. Why was this man not located? If he deceived the government by false affidavits, there is no reason whatever why he should not have been prosecuted. Why has something not been done, why is he immune, having defrauded the government of Canada under false declarations? Why is he immune when not one scintilla of evidence is available that even the slightest interest was taken by the Department of Public Works to ascertain the whereabouts of the wrongdoer? He was living in a Regina hotel. All these tradesmen were defrauded as a result of a false declaration. Over six weeks ago I had a question passed as an order for return asking that the declaration be produced. There is no one else who can prosecute Lunam except the government which was defrauded. The workmen, the suppliers of the goods, can do nothing. All they are met with is, "Well, if he owes you money why don't you sue him?" We have a straw man and a straw company.
Mr. Speaker, these are circumstances that merit the serious attention of parliament. If


men and women in this country cannot deal as subcontractors with safety, there is no safety for anyone in connection with government contracts. I could continue at length in this regard. I referred to the generally evasive nature of the letters received by the subcontractors in Saskatchewan when they asked the government for action. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) says, we dealt with these contracts in the ordinary way. If they did, and I accept that statement as I accept the Prime Minister's statements, then there is something radically wrong with the whole system in the Department of Public Works. There is no way in which this matter can be brought out except through the instrumentality of a select committee of parliament to look into it.
I do not know whether or not there are other cases, but I have placed on the order paper, returnable on Thursday next, a question regarding the post office at Southampton, Ontario. If my informants have given me the correct information, the answer to these questions, too, will reveal that a real shake-up is necessary in order to preserve, on the one hand the rights of government, and on the other hand the rights of individuals in this country who deal with the government.
Mention is made by the Prime Minister of the fact that a number of contracts had been completed successfully by the Lunam Construction Company before Mr. Lunam suffered this accident.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That may be so, but I did not make that statement; and I do not know whether it is true or not.
All right. I may have misunderstood the Prime Minister, and I hasten to make a correction if I have done so. That was the inference I drew from his statement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What I said was that my information was that there were some of these contracts that would be completed for less than the amount remaining unpaid to Lunam, that there would therefore be a surplus, that there had been some suggestion that that surplus might be applied to other contracts where there was a deficit, and that I did not think that would be fair.

I accept the correction, and I say this. According to the Minister of Public Works there will be approximately $3,500 to the credit of Lunam. What then is the situation? Approximately $239,000 worth of materials that have not been paid for have gone into these buildings that the government of Canada has taken over, a fact which indicates that there was waste or carelessness in the construction by Lunam and that there

was not that degree of supervision on the part of the Department of Public Works that is necessary in order to protect the taxpayers' dollar and to assure as well protection for individuals dealing with contractors.
The post office building in Prince Albert was built by this contractor. It was completed a long while ago. Yet there are contractors in Prince Albert who have not received anything on account of the work. Here is the situation of one firm in Prince Albert. Haylor and Hogeweide, a painting and decorating firm in Prince Albert, according to their statement here, have $3,801 coming for painting and decorating done. They state that they put in their claim but that they have never been paid. Lunam was paid for the work these people did. No wonder he could keep within his contract price; and even in the completion of the work that remains to be done on some of his contracts, it will be possible to complete them within the limitations of the tender he made. But $3,500 divided among the creditors of this contractor is as nothing.
I suggest that the Prime Minister might well accept the suggestion-although he has turned the question down without going into it at length-of a thorough investigation, because this is the first time that the curtain has been lifted in even the slightest degree. If this be the regular system, then changes must be made. The changes must be made for the future in order to protect the Canadian people. They must also be made to protect honest dealers who deal with contractors and who believe that those contractors will be required to live within and to maintain each and every portion of the contracts they enter into. Such a special committee of parliament could be similar to the one that was recommended by Sir Wilfrid Laurier many years ago.
These are matters that affect all Canadians. I say to the government: Set up a committee such as that which is suggested. Let us have the answers to the questions which I asked weeks ago and which have not been answered. Let us ascertain whether there are not material changes that must be made in the awarding of contracts and in the preservation of the rights of individuals dealing with contractors, both being necessary in order to achieve the largest possible return for the money to be expended by parliament and at the same time protecting those Canadians who have a right to be protected. There is no way under law by which they can be protected except by a strong, stern, severe supervision by those in authority in the Department of Public
29, 1953	4535
Lunam Construction Company Works or in the other departments of government, before payments are made to a contractor in respect of services or materials that have been supplied to him.
I am not going to say anything more at this time. Today the Lunam Construction Company owes at least 40 firms in Saskatchewan. Its record appears in some detail in the return brought down as sessional paper No. 178 on February 11, wherein are set forth in detail the contracts this company had and those wherein it has defaulted. It defaulted in the department of Indian affairs. It defaulted in the Department of Public Works. It did not default in the Department of Defence Production. Apparently one department was able to ensure that proper auditing took place, whereas in two other departments there was not that degree of supervision and examination which Canadians have a right to expect.
I join with the Leader of the Opposition in support of the motion, because I know how necessary it is that Canadians have a realization of what is taking place and what methods must be achieved in order to protect the taxpayers' dollar.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alphonse Fournier (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am to a certain extent pleased to see that some interest has been developed in the activities of the Department of Public Works. I have been head of that department for nearly eleven years now. During that time I recall that this house has voted for that department millions of dollars in the space of an hour or so. That procedure kept on until this year. I was grateful to hon. members for their confidence in the officials of the department and in myself; and I am convinced that, when I am through making these few remarks, the officials of the department and I will still have the esteem and confidence of the members of the house.
May I thank the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), the leaders of the other parties, and also my friend the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) for the tone in which they treated this subject before the house. The motion was for an inquiry into the procedure of the Department of Public Works, as to the way contracts are awarded and as to what happened in the Lunam case. I suggest that all that can be explained by myself just as well as it could be explained by an official of the department if he were to appear before a committee. The last paragraph, as the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) stated, seems to be quite out of order. Nobody believes that the government has failed in the execution of its public works in the last eleven years. This is the first time it has been suggested.
4536	HOUSE OF
Lunam Construction Company
The Leader of the Opposition wants to know how we proceed in public works. May I say that we proceed in an extremely simple manner. We follow the statute that governs the department and we follow the contracts we sign with contractors. Those are the binding limits on our activities. I have the statute before me. It has been discussed in this house. Hon. members know that if I was advised sometimes to ask for amendments that did not meet the wishes of the house I was the first one to admit that the amendment should be amended. It went so far that one hon. gentleman said that he had brought me down to my knees to amend the amendment. I did not have to be brought down to my knees. I was using only good sense, after consulting members of parliament, members of the opposition and everybody else. I think we have a good statute.
I believe there is a lot of red tape in that statute, and I have always approved of it, because it is the one spending department that exists and has existed since the British North America Act was passed. It has been developed in the decades by different governments, and it was set out in the statute books until two years ago, when we found that the value of the dollar was not the same as it was in 1867. At that time I obtained an increase in the amount of contracts that could be awarded without public tenders from $5,000 to $15,000. That is the only amendment in the eleven years that I have been head of this department.
What does the act say about the general procedure? This was debated in the house by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew). I cannot recall whether the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) took part but I do recall that the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) put up quite a struggle against section 36 of the Public Works Act being amended, or if amended there should be a limit on the amount. We took probably two days on that question. Never was it mentioned that I did not follow the statute or follow the binding procedure in the giving out of contracts.
We followed that in all of the Lunam cases. I have given answers to questions that were put to me by the hon. member for Lake Centre. They will be found in Hansard of January 26, 1953, at page 1309 as follows:
How many contracts for buildings or projects have been let by the Department of Public Works to the Lunam Construction Company, in Saskatchewan, since January 1, 1948?
The answer I gave was:
Eight:	Prince Albert; Regina; Tisdale; Fort
Qu'Appelle; Langenburg; Fort Qu'Appelle; Regina; Fort Qu'Appelle.


There were two buildings at Regina, and at Fort Qu'Appelle an Indian hospital. I gave the amounts of the contracts; I gave the amounts that were paid; I named the buildings that had been completed and paid for, and I mentioned that three buildings had not been completed.
When we met with this case of Lunam in February, 1952, I was advised by my officials that this man had discontinued the execution of work on certain buildings and that we were receiving certain claims. I instructed them to withhold any payments, to communicate with the contractor and tell him that if the works were not resumed and completed according to the terms of his contract the department would take over. That is one of the clauses of the contract between Her Majesty and jhe contractor. We had up to that time received, to my personal knowledge and according to the information I am given, no criticism of Lunam or his company.
When the hon. gentleman says that we should have looked into Lunam's background as a contractor, well, lately somebody told me that years ago he had been an employee of the Poole Construction Company which had fallen by the wayside. Now, I ask myself if that would be a reason to take him off the list of tenders that were made according to the statute?
This morning the Leader of the Opposition was kind enough to tell me that in 1948 this contractor had started a job but had not completed it. I must admit that neither my officials nor I knew about it, or if they did, I did not know that he had had troubles. But if I look back into the history of this department I find that one of the largest contractors in Canada had failed in putting up one of the largest buildings in the capital city. Who blamed the Department of Public Works at the time? Nobody blames the department because a contractor fails. I am mixed up with bankruptcies. I can give a case in the city of Sherbrooke where a contractor failed. He was declared bankrupt; a trustee was appointed. The trustee undertook to complete the work. He has just completed the work, and we shall hand back to that trustee the amount of the security deposit and the amount that we had held back on the execution of the contract. That is the regular procedure in public works. Is it perfect? Well, it is just as perfect as any other system of contracting on buildings that I have seen.
We have a guarantee but no bond, as the hon. gentleman says. During the years it was found that a security deposit in cash of 10 per cent, plus a holdback of 10 per cent on the execution of the works, was a sufficient guarantee, and I admit that we have not lost

much money. Everything that was regular in all the contracts I have been handling for eleven years was followed in the case of Lunam, who was the lowest tenderer, who had the equipment, the personnel and the experience. Even if he had worked for firms that had failed, he must have had experience, for away back in 1931 he was one of the foremen or head men of that Poole Construction Company. Therefore we could not say that he did not have the knowledge and the experience; we could not say that he did not have the financial backing. He put up the deposit, as is done in every case. We could not say that we were not protecting the public treasury by holding back the 10 per cent.
I sincerely ask any hon. member, were he Minister of Public Works, what he would have advised in the Lunam case that I have not undertaken, to protect the public treasury. My duty here, and according to the statute, representing the people of the country, is to see that when I give a contract I get the services on the work that is mentioned in that contract in the value agreed on and put up by this parliament on the request of the Minister of Public Works.
In every instance in the Lunam case I am told that we have value for the money that was expended. Perhaps today I am the only defender of the public treasury, when I see my hon. friend trying to protect creditors who may have lost money on certain contracts. They have little experience if they believe that nobody loses money on contracts, even subcontractors. Nobody sympathizes more than I when I see a contractor fail; but my sympathy has to be displaced in the observance of the statute, and so long as I am holding this portfolio my first duty, and what I will do, is to protect the public treasury. I shall make mistakes; I make them every day even in this house; my officials will make mistakes. But up to date nobody has charged anybody in that department with wrongdoing. If they were doing wrong it has not come to my attention; and if there is wrongdoing those who are the wrongdoers will in one way or another pay for it.
That is the position we take in the department. With respect to the officials who have been in that department so long, and who are respected, and who deserve the respect of the population, I wish to give them credit for the work they have been doing ever since I have been Minister of Public Works.
With regard to the protection of creditors, I am all for it. Do not put the crown over and above the ordinary private man, says the hon. member for Lake Centre. But would the hon. member for Lake Centre tell me why no storekeeper or anybody else around here
29, 1953
Lunam Construction Company can garnishee the wages of a civil servant? Is that the difference between the crown and the ordinary man? And this has the approval of parliament, and has had it for years.
We are not spending here the money of one person; we are spending the people's money. And every statute which is passed here is to protect the public treasury under the supervision of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), the comptroller of the treasury, the treasury board and the Auditor General, all these who protect the public treasury. If I were doing things or if my officials were doing things by which the country would lose money, then I think I could be justly blamed. But the argument used now by the hon. member for Lake Centre is, "You should protect these subcontractors, these people who sell materials." Well, if I had the time, probably I would do that. If I could go around to all the contracts we are handling in the Department of Public Works to see if that keg of nails in Peterborough was paid for, or if this other thing somewhere else was paid for-well, if I did that, I do not know whether I could administer the department at all. That is not the way it is done.
But $240,000 is not a keg of nails.

If we did nothing, why not tell me? We have not been told anything. The hon. member wants to know where we stand. Well, if he will just wait until we get through with this contract we will know exactly where we stand with Mr. Lunam, and perhaps with his creditors.
