the guarantees with Lunam are those which have been followed for years and years, even before I was Minister of Public Works.
We have followed that practice in each instance. And having done that, without waiting to complete the discussion that our case is well prepared, my hon. friend comes to the House of Commons. I can tell you this, that it is no help either to the officials of my department or to the claimants to have the matter decided on the floor of the House of Commons. My hon. friend might make a good judge, but when he is in parliament he loses sight of the facts and makes a political speech. I would not want my department to be subjected to that; I would rather have the case come up before the courts.
The country will lose no money in this transaction, through the Department of Public Works. I tell my hon. friend that if I can give him any information and I can say anything else to prove that my department has rendered good service for so many years, with the limited money it has had to expend, I shall do so. Since the last war hon. members can see what it has been doing throughout this country, in nearly every constituency. And I am still proud of what my department has done with the amount of money granted to it by parliament.

Mr. Speaker, there are two or three points with which I should like to deal for a few moments, arising out of the remarks just made by the Minister of Public Works. He did not explain, in the first place, the fact that when his department suspended payment to the Lunam Construction Company Limited, which I believe was in December, no notification of that action was given to any of the subcontractors.
The minister has said that he notified the main contractor, the Lunam Construction Company Limited. But he makes no pretence of having notified the subtrades of that position, that the Lunam people were no longer responsible and that the government was to make no further payments to them. That I think is where one of the grave injustices in this matter arises. I believe that at least some of the subtrades, after the time the minister suspended payment to the Lunam Construction Company Limited, supplied materials on the jobs. They incurred further expenses, the benefit of which went to the government.
During that time they had not been notified that the government was no longer making payments to Lunam. The result of course was that the government got the benefit of these

materials that were supplied and, in actual fact, got the goods for nothing, at the expense of these subtrades.
I suggest that that is a very unfair situation. The Minister of Public Works has made no attempt whatever to justify that result. In fact he has taken the position this afternoon that he was not interested in the subtrades, that they were none of his responsibility, that he was only dealing with the head contractor, the Lunam Construction Company Limited. Yet we find him making a statement on April 8, as reported on page 3618 of Hansard. While he says today that he had no interest whatever in the subtrades, that they were none of his responsibility, he told us at that time that he was getting reports every month from his inspectors on the job about the firms who were actually supplying these materials and the men who had subcontracts. I quote from one paragraph on that page as follows:
Every month, on special dates, a contractor makes progress reports as to the work done and the materials employed, and gives us a list of those who have sold him materials,. That list is part of the progress report, and it is accompanied by an affidavit of the contractor.
I was wrong in saying that he got those reports from his inspectors. He got them from the head contractor. If the minister's statement on April 8 was correct, those reports contained a list of the subcontractors and of the people who were supplying materials. So all the way through the minister was in a position to contact these subtrades. When he knew the head contractor was no longer able to function, the minister had the opportunity to notify the subtrades, but I believe there was no notification whatever sent to them for a matter of two or three months after he had suspended payments to Lunam Construction Company Limited.
Then I understand that the department took the holdback and the deposit from jobs that had been completed and used them to complete jobs which had not been completed. SureL' that was an unfair procedure. If a man has supplied materials for building A and that building has been completed and there is money held by the government, what right does the minister have to take the money which he is holding in that case, and rather than using it to pay the man who has helped complete the job, take it and use it to finish another job?

People sent in their bills to the contractor who, in his affidavit, swore that they were paid. Up to that time there was no difficulty at all, and no claim from anyone. On April 8 the Minister of Public Works went on to boast that with the money which had been taken as holdbacks and security the government had been able to complete the other jobs. He boasted of that on April 8. The fact is that his position

Lunam Construction Company
is entirely different from the position taken today by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Why is not there a trustee in bankruptcy who sees to it that these things are done?

It is not the job of the trustee in bankruptcy to see that the government does its duty or acts fairly. That is the responsibility of the government, not of any trustee in bankruptcy. There is another feature which the Minister of Public Works did not explain; and I regret to see he has had to leave the house.
Minister of Public Works, as appears at page 3620 of Hansard for April 8, and at one point he said in reply:
When we make a progress payment it is to enable him to pay these bills, and he swears he has paid them.
I suggest that is putting the cart before the horse. The contractor should be required to produce his receipts before he is paid. If that were done, then there would be no unfortunate occurrences such as in this case. For these reasons I suggest that a committee should be appointed and a new system should be worked out for the handling of construction contracts of this kind.
The fact is that there was not adequate supervision of these jobs. If a private individual had a contract of this kind with an architect employed, that architect would see the receipts showing that the subtrades had been paid. In these cases the minister was getting lists of subtrades all the time. There was an architect at least on some jobs, and I presume there were also inspectors. Yet nobody seems to have accepted any responsibility for seeing that the contractor paid the subtrades.
When this was under discussion on April 8 the Minister of Public Works took the position that that was quite all right, that he had no responsibility in that regard, and in effect said that if the subtrades did not get paid it was just too bad for them. I suggest that shows a serious defect in the manner in which the Department of Public Works is functioning on these jobs. The very fact that ;he department is supposed to get affidavits from the contractor showing that he has made payments indicates that it was the intention of parliament throughout that the subtrades should be protected, that proof should be required of payment of the bills of these subcontractors. Yet that practice has not been followed at all by the Department of Public Works.
I think the great value of this amendment lies in the fact that it asks for an investigation of this situation in the hope that there will be a better system worked out for supervising government contracts. There surely would be very little difficulty in having the government make a contractor produce his receipts before paying. Instead of doing that in this case, as the Minister of Public Works indicated during the discussion on April 8, the money was actually paid out to the Lunam Construction Company Limited so that they could pay their debts. Administration service-
1. Departmental administration, $358,893.

Mr. Chairman, when this item was up for consideration before, on Monday evening, the Minister of Agriculture did something which I think is rather unprecedented in the House of Commons. He read into the record a copy of a letter which he had written to the premier of Saskatchewan with regard to the South Saskatchewan river dam and report. The letter was dated the previous Friday, and I have since learned that this letter was written by the hon. gentleman on April 24 in Regina and was delivered to the premier of Saskatchewan at his home on Monday evening at ten o'clock, Regina time, or two hours after the letter had been made public in the House of Commons.
As I understand it, the procedure that has been followed in the house for a long time now has been this. When letters are exchanged between a minister and the government of a province, when we have asked for even the production of that correspondence we have always been told that the correspondence could not be tabled or be made public until the consent of the other government had been received. In this instance, for what purpose I do not know, a letter was delivered at Premier Douglas' home in Regina at ten o'clock, Regina time, on Monday evening, over two hours after the communication had been read in the House of Commons. I say that that act seems to me to be one of discourtesy, having regard to the procedure that we have followed in the house now for a long time.
I know the Minister of Agriculture has little use for the present government of Saskatchewan and never misses an opportunity to show that fact, as he did this morning, for example, when he interjected quite irrelevantly the statement that the Conservative party and the C.C.F. had in some way co-operated last year in the provincial election. Let me remind him that in 1948 a coalition was formed between my hon. friend's supporters in the province of Saskatchewan and the Conservative party, so that the Conservatives delivered the votes and the Liberals got the seats. There was indeed one independent Conservative elected, and that independent Conservative is today a member of the Liberal party. I do not know whether or not he was in fact an independent Conservative at the time he was elected to the legislature of Saskatchewan.
I want to say something both about this letter and about the matter of the Saskatchewan river dam, particularly as it closely affects my own constituency. In the event of irrigation being undertaken on the South

Supply-Agriculture
Saskatchewan river, it would be the constituency of Rosetown-Biggar that would largely benefit from the undertaking.
This subject has been a matter of discussion in the House of Commons and in the country for a number of years. I recall raising the matter here myself in 1938 and moving a resolution asking for the study of irrigation possibilities in Saskatchewan and indeed in western Canada. From time to time the Minister of Agriculture himself has made speeches in which he has fairly clearly indicated to the people of Saskatchewan that the project would be undertaken. But when I look at this letter which the hon. gentleman wrote on April 24 to the premier of Saskatchewan, I find that he now takes a position entirely different, as I shall show in a moment, from the position that has been taken hitherto either by himself or by the government. He says:
. . . the federal government is prepared to consider a definite proposal from the provincial government for co-operation in the project and I am authorized by my colleagues to discuss such a proposal with you-
That is with Premier Douglas.
-once the question of water rights has been settled among the three prairie provinces and agreement reached that the water would be available for the project.
He also goes on to say this:
Any proposal put forward by the province should make it clear what contribution to the cost of the dam itself the province is prepared to make to remove any element of federal subsidy for the production of power since power development could obviously not be subsidized in one province . . .
Of course power development could not be subsidized in one province. But the Prime Minister, when he was speaking in the house on February 9 of this year, said something rather different in discussing the project in reply to a question of my friend the hon. member for Lake Centre. The hon. member for Lake Centre said, "What proof is required for that?"-that is, if the Prime Minister could be convinced to the point where he could honestly say that he believed it to be the best use of the water. The Prime Minister then went on to say this, as reported at page 1770 of Hansard:
I do not know of any better use.
That is better use of the water.
But they suggest-
Referring to the experts who have just reported.
-and they are experts, I am not-that that further information is required to reach a positive opinion as to whether or not that is the best use. I think it would be a good use. I am not frightened at the cost.

Then further down he goes on to say:
-the creation of that body of water in the province of Saskatchewan would be a magnificent thing, and that the indirect, not the direct returns -the direct returns you cannot calculate mathematically-would be a permanent addition to the capital value of this great country of ours.
In his letter the Minister of Agriculture makes no mention of the use of the water or the desirability of convincing the government of Canada and the Prime Minister that this would be the best use. What he says is that he would like to get the views of the Saskatchewan government and the proposals that government may have in this regard.
Let us take a look at the background of this matter, to some extent, and see what actually has happened in connection with proposals dealing with this matter. For example, in 1950 the Minister of Agriculture made the statement in the House of Commons that he was meeting the Saskatchewan government to discuss the South Saskatchewan river project. At that time the government of Saskatchewan had heard nothing about such a meeting; so on June 19 the premier of Saskatchewan sent this telegram to the minister:
Notice you have stated in House of Commons that you are meeting government latter part of this week. None of the Saskatchewan ministers have received any word of proposed meeting. We are anxious to make sure that members of cabinet are available to suit your convenience. Would you advise us if you desire meeting and if so please suggest date.
In reply to that telegram the minister wired as follows:
Retel. I regret not having previously contacted you. Will be in Regina Saturday morning, June 24. Wish to discuss with you and members of your government, particularly ministers of finance and agriculture, the South Saskatchewan project and possible financial arrangements.
The premier of Saskatchewan wired back:
Meeting arranged for 9 a.m., Saturday, June 24, office of provincial treasurer.
That meeting was held and a discussion took place, but apparently no definite arrangement or decision was made. Then on January 15, 1951 the Minister of Agriculture wrote to the premier of Saskatchewan and said:
I have been wondering whether it would be possible sometime during the day of February 2 to have further discussions on the possible development of the South Saskatchewan river project. If so, I shall make time available for that purpose.
I expect to arrive in Regina on February 1 by plane and to leave by train on Saturday, February 3.
Then we have the reply thanking the minister for the letter of January 15. Then a reference to the possibility of discussing the South Saskatchewan river project, as follows:
I am sure that my colleagues and I would be prepared to arrange our schedule so as to meet

you at your convenience when you are in the province on February 1 and 2. As you have said, the sitting on Friday afternoon is usually quite brief, and the ceremony in connection with the hanging of your portrait will not likely take more than half an hour. This means that we could have a meeting from four to six in the afternoon, unless you have some other plans. If, however, you would prefer the morning, we would do our best to arrange it although I think four to six p.m. would be more convenient for us.
Trusting you will advise me of your wishes in this matter and looking forward to seeing you when you are in Regina.
Then we have the reply to that:
I expect to be in Regina on Wednesday the 24th.
The meeting was held, and some * definite arrangements regarding the project were agreed upon. As a result the premier of Saskatchewan immediately put in writing the understandings that had been arrived at and sent them to the minister. Because this letter is quite important, in view of the project under discussion, I want to put it all on the record. This is from the premier's office in Regina; it is dated February 10, 1951, and reads:
Dear Mr. Gardiner:
This will confirm the conversations which took place between you and the members of the Saskatchewan government on Friday afternoon, February 2.
Our understanding is that the federal government is prepared to accept full responsibility for the construction of the dam-
There is no reservation in that. I continue:
-the estimated cost of which is to be in the neighbourhood of $68 million. It was further suggested that the distribution system at an estimated cost of $19 million and the cost of levelling the land for irrigation, which is estimated at $6 million were to be the responsibility of the provincial government and the water users who will benefit by this project. It was also suggested that the installations for the generation of hydroelectric power at an estimated cost of $8 million were to be the exclusive responsibility of the provincial government. While this is not the allocation of costs which was suggested when this project was first proposed, if this is the only basis on which the federal government is prepared to proceed with the project, I do not see that we have any alternative than to base our discussions on the allocation which you outlined to us-

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: "To base our discussions."

The letter continues:
[DOT]-which you outlined to us (on February 2, 1951). My colleagues and I are most anxious that the South Saskatchewan river development project shall be proceeded with at the earliest possible date. As soon as the federal government has announced its intention to proceed with this undertaking, we are prepared to negotiate and sign an agreement on the basis of the allocation of costs outlined above. You were good enough to suggest that this allocation of costs was not to be considered as final but merely the basis for future negotiations. It is understood that if any more favourable terms are given any other province, for example, the St. Mary's project in Alberta, Saskatchewan would receive similar treatment.
Supply-Agriculture
May I say how pleased we were to have the opportunity of discussing this matter with you and may I express the hope that in view of the agreement contained in this letter, it will be possible to proceed with the construction of the South Saskatchewan river development project some time during the present year.
The present year was, of course, 1951. There was an acknowledgment from the minister's private secretary as follows:
In Mr. Gardiner's absence this will acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 10th February, which will he brought to his attention upon his return.
There was no further communication. The minister did not reply to this letter, and it was quite obvious that the understanding reached at the meeting of February 2 was an understanding on both sides.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I replied to that letter in June.

Yes, in June. The next letter was dated June 26. Had there been any doubt in the minister's mind as to the correctness of the statement made by the premier of Saskatchewan in February, I have no doubt the minister would have written at once to correct any misunderstanding. On June 26 the minister wrote as follows:
I am sorry when going over our files to find that I did not answer your letter of February 10, 1951.
I note that you indicate in your letter that your government is prepared to consider an expenditure of $25 million on the irrigation system and $8 million for the generation of hydro electric power if the federal government would undertake to build a dam across the South Saskatchewan river near Outlook at an estimated cost of $68 million. I note that as soon as the federal government has announced its intention to proceed with this undertaking your government is prepared to negotiate and sign an agreement on the basis of the above allocation of costs.
There has been considerable discussion on the question since, some of which has found its way on to Hansard and some of which has taken place through the press.
It has been recently announced that all the information available with regard to the proposed South Saskatchewan development will be placed before a committee of experts and their opinion obtained before final consideration is given to the proposed development. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) stated to the house today that he hoped to be able to announce the personnel of the committee of experts at an early date.
I may say that in checking the records here I find that none of the three prairie provinces have yet notified us that they are agreed upon the division of water proposed by the provincial-dominion water board. I am sure you will agree that it will be necessary for us to have the opinions of the three governments before final consideration can be given to the matter.
I hope favourable decision will have been made to the findings of the water board by the time the committee has given its opinion on the whole development.
There we get a fairly complete background of the part that Saskatchewan was prepared

Supply-Agriculture
to play and the understanding which in February, 1951, seemed to be understood was agreeable to both sides. Of course, that letter caused a good deal of consternation among those of us who were interested in the project, the setting up of another commission to go into the many reports on this project that have already been made to the house and to the government. It also caused us some anxiety, because we understood that the minister's own advisers in the P.F.R.A. had made estimates of the costs and recommendations for the location of the dam, and that everything was ready to proceed when this commission was set up.
I have always been rather surprised that when that commission was set up there were two power project men and only one irrigation man on the commission in the person of Dr. Widtsoe. Unfortunately, Dr. Widtsoe fell ill. He was a man in whom I learned to have confidence as an irrigation expert, because although I did not know anything about him until he was appointed to the commission, subsequently I saw some of his writings and learned something of his record, and I must say that he commanded my confidence. Unfortunately he was an aged man. He fell ill. He underwent an operation which was serious for an aged man. He died before he could complete the work he was called upon to do.
The appointment of this commission of course provoked a letter from the premier of Saskatchewan and again I wish to put it on the record, because I think the record should be complete. It is dated at Regina, August 2, 1951 and reads:
Dear Mr. Gardiner:
I have your letter of June 26 in regard to the South Saskatchewan irrigation and power project. You will recall that this was in reply to my letter of February 10, in which I advised that as a result of our earlier conversations with you the Saskatchewan government was prepared to enter into an agreement on the sharing of financial responsibility along the lines indicated in my letter, in order that an early start might be made on the project.
I now note that the government of Canada is appointing a committee to review all the information on the project and that the Prime Minister expects shortly to announce the personnel of the committee. We feel sure that you will agree that the data which has already been compiled by competent engineers and technicians has provided conclusive evidence that the project is both practical and feasible. Dr. L. B. Thomson, of P.F.E.A., has in fact expressed to us the view that no irrigation project in Canada has ever been so thoroughly and carefully documented as this proposal. We cannot appreciate the need for this further review, but are of course prepared to co-operate with the committee in any way we possibly can to expedite their work.
In your letter you mention that none of the three prairie provinces have yet notified you "that

they are agreed upon the division of water proposed by the provincial-dominion water board". You will, of course, be aware that the recommendation of the board with respect to allocations for certain projects in Alberta have now been formally assented to by all four participating governments. Our own application for an allocation of water for the South Saskatchewan project has been before the board since May, 1949. The documents and evidence submitted since then in support of the requested allocation are admittedly far more complete and authoritative than any other application previously accepted by the board. The Saskatchewan government withheld formal assent to the Alberta allocations only until such time as authoritative water studies by the board itself showed that the supply of water is adequate for the needs of projects in all three provinces. We have now issued the required order in council with the distinct understanding that an early meeting of the board will be called to recommend a final allocation for the South Saskatchewan project. It is inconceivable that this will not be forthcoming.
In any event, as you well know, construction of the St. Mary's dam, opened by yourself only two weeks ago, was begun by the federal government at least three years prior to formal agreement by all the provinces on the water allocation. In fact, very substantial works had been carried out on the project by the federal government long before an agreement had been finalized with the province of Alberta.
In view of the foregoing, we cannot see that any further delay is necessary. We would urge again that the government of Canada should recognize its obligations in this matter and undertake the immediate construction of this project which will undoubtedly benefit the nation as a whole and Saskatchewan in particular.
I hope favourable decision will have been made to the findings of the water board by the time the committee has given its opinion on the whole development.
That is signed by Mr. Douglas. Then the investigation went on. Some of us in the house were pressing for the presentation of the report. Early in the session of 1952 a question was placed on the order paper by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson) asking if the Saskatchewan government had presented a brief. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) answered that no brief'had been presented.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member if he is not going to put my other letter on the record, so that it will be complete? There is one further letter.

I thought I had all the letters. Perhaps I just missed that one, and failed to bring it down to the chamber. However, a reply was given by the Prime Minister-and I absolve him from responsibility in making it, because it was not according to the facts. I suppose his officials drafted it for him. Mr. Douglas saw the Prime Minister's reply in Hansard and, accordingly, wrote to him on March 28, 1952 as follows:
My dear Prime Minister:
In answer to a question placed on the order paper by Mr. Larson, member for Kindersley, you are

quoted as stating that the Saskatchewan government has not yet presented a brief to the royal commission investigating the South Saskatchewan river project despite the fact that the chairman of the said commission requested us to do so on December 19.
It seems to me that in all fairness the House of Commons should have been informed that the Saskatchewan government met two members of the royal commission informally on September 21, 1951, and that at that time our technical staff discussed with the secretary and two members of the commission the type of information they required and the scope of the inquiry. During the latter part of December we were informed that the chairman of the commission had to return to Salt Lake City and that one member of the commission was ill and that consequently we could carry on further investigations before making our submission. On March 12, 1952, Mr. B. T. Richardson-
He was secretary of the commission.
-informed our technical staff that the royal commission was not satisfied with the estimates furnished by the P.F.R.A. and that a meeting of the engineering consultants was being held in Washington, D.C., on April 7. Mr. Richardson invited the Saskatchewan government to send an engineer to the proposed meeting and stated that our report should be withheld until the results of this conference were made known. Mr. Richardson's statements of March 12 have since been confirmed in a letter dated March 22.
Then Mr. Douglas goes on to say what is perfectly correct-
There is no provincial government in Canada which has co-operated more fully with the royal commission investigating the South Saskatchewan river project than has the government of Saskatchewan. We have indicated our willingness to place before them all the data which we have and to carry out extensive investigations regarding any matters on which they want further information. Any attempt to suggest that the Saskatchewan government has not co-operated fully is not in accordance with the facts and cannot possibly serve the best interests of the investigation which you initiated. If the government of Canada wants us to file a submission without waiting for the results of the proposed conference in Washington on April 7 we shall, of course, comply. We thought, however, that by acceding to the request of the secretary of the commission that we wait until certain information had been received from consulting engineers we were acting in accordance with the wish of the commission.
Then he goes on to add:
I do not propose to have the Saskatchewan government placed in the impossible position ol being blamed inferentially for not having submitted a report, while at the same time the commission itself is suggesting that we withhold our submission until after the results of the conference commencing April 7 are made known to us. I would therefore appreciate hearing from you as to whether or not you wish our submission filed immediately or whether you prefer to have us withhold it as requested by the commission.
That is pretty much the story of the negotiations as they occurred, and the attempt from time to time to transfer the responsibility for delay from the federal to the provincial government. The provincial government, and hon. members in the House of
Supply-Agriculture
Commons who are from Saskatchewan, particularly those in the vicinity of the river, have done everything possible to co-operate in bringing this great project to a successful conclusion.
I believe this is a project which would be of inestimable value to the people of my province and, indeed, to the people of Canada. I agree with the Prime Minister when he says that he does not know of a better use that could be made of that water. I agree with him when he says that this great body of water in the centre of Saskatchewan should be available for irrigation, and incidentally available to supply water to the cities of Moose Jaw and Regina, although of course that must not be made a main consideration because this is an irrigation rather than a water project. However, it is a very important feature of the proposal.
Premier Douglas has again assured the Prime Minister when, first of all, he states that he is in receipt of a letter from the Minister of Agriculture asking the provincial government to submit a proposal for the construction of the South Saskatchewan dam. He says this, and I think quite properly, in view of all that has happened:
Before submitting proposal or discussing agreement essential that we have from you-
That is from the Prime Minister.
-categorical assurance on two points-
They are reasonable points.
-first that you are now convinced that South Saskatchewan river project represents best use that can be made of water available and secondly that the federal government is prepared to proceed with this undertaking if government of Saskatchewan assumes fair share of costs.
Premier Douglas says they have always been prepared to assume a fair share of the costs. As a matter of fact I can imagine that hon. members from Saskatchewan were quite disappointed in the report of the royal commission. We could not be otherwise. How that decision of the commission was arrived at I find it difficult to understand. I noticed that when the report was first issued the Minister of Agriculture made some very caustic comments regarding the report as made by that commission to the government, although he denied some of the language that was attributed to him.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister called it a silly blank, blank report.

I know that is what was in the press, but I can only guess what the "blank, blank" stands for. In view of the fact that this is a navigable stream the damming of the river is a federal project, and

Supply-Agriculture
the cost and allocation of the cost were discussed with the government of Saskatchewan in 1951. Any further proposal to vary this should not be requested from the province of Saskatchewan but should come from the federal government. If they have any further suggestions to make regarding costs and allocation of costs, it is the federal authority and not the provincial authority that should take the initiative. Moreover, it is the federal authority which has all the engineering and other details, all the estimates and everything else in connection with this project.
I suppose that with an election coming along and the disappointment there is in Saskatchewan, the Minister of Agriculture is anxious to prolong the discussion and place the responsibility where it certainly does not lie. I am not going to be a party to that, and I am sure the government of the province of Saskatchewan will not be a party to that kind of thing. This project is too big to play politics with. I do not think anyone can accuse me of ever playing politics with this important project, and I do not intend to do that either now or in the future. I hope the Minister of Agriculture will not be able to introduce a political angle into this.
There is an election coming and a definite proposal is up to the federal authority and none other. A tentative agreement having been reached, and this being a navigable river under the jurisdiction of the federal authority there has never at any time until recently been any suggestion that the province should be called upon to do more than was agreed to at Regina on February 9, 1951. I have tried to place the facts before the committee. The minister says I have omitted a letter. If I did so it was done quite inadvertently and I shall be glad to have the minister complete the record.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Did the hon. member read the letter of August 15, 1951?
I thought I had all the correspondence with me. Did I not read it?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The premier's letter was dated August 2 and I replied on August 15. I do not think the hon. member read that letter.
I may have it in a separate file for some reason. Perhaps the minister would complete the record in that respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I just reply to one or two things before we go on to some other matter. Statements have been made with regard to the letter that was prepared and sent to the premier of Saskatchewan under date of April 24, and it was suggested that I must have written this

letter in Regina on April 24. Perhaps I should review some of the history of the discussions that have been going on. It will be recalled that when we were discussing this matter some time ago-
May I ask the minister why that letter was delivered by messenger and not mailed.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I shall come to that. When the matter was being discussed here previously, one of the questions that came up was whether we had discussed the matter and whether this government was going to build the South Saskatchewan river dam. I stated that it was not discussed in 1951 at the time the proposal was before the government, and that it was not discussed again when the report of the commission was received.
I think it follows that before I wrote the letter that was written to Premier Douglas the question certainly was discussed. We had continuous discussions in council about it and finally the letter which I sent to Premier Douglas was passed upon by council. It constitutes the present policy of the government in relation to the South Saskatchewan dam.
That statement of government policy was dealt with in the manner in which statements of government policy always have been dealt with in this house. Had I made the announcement when I was in Regina or had I made it in any other place but this House of Commons I would have been strongly criticized for having done so. This was an important matter of policy having to do with a most important question, and for me to have gone to Regina and made the announcement there before the Canadian Club, to which I happened to be speaking on April 24, I am certain would not have been acceptable to the leader of the C.C.F. party, nor would it have been-
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Just let me finish the story and I think you will be satisfied. I do not think it would have been satisfactory to the members of any other section of the house had I done that. When I was speaking on February 24 to the Canadian Club in Regina I said that had the matter been dealt with in the house prior to my coming there I would have dealt with it at that time, that that would have been the subject of my speech. But as it had not been dealt with and as it would be necessary for me to deliver any message I had to the house before discussing it outside, I told them it would be impossible for me to discuss it at that particular time. I said I would be discussing it here in the course of a few days.	.

But I left a sealed copy of the letter I desired to have delivered with Mr. L. B. Thomson, commissioner of the P.F.R.A. I asked him when I rose in the house to deliver my speech, which I thought would be at about 11 o'clock in the morning-it was about 9 o'clock in the evening-to personally deliver the letter to Mr. Douglas and tell him the reason he had not had it before, that I was making my announcement on the floor of the house and intended him to have it before I read it to the house. That is why it was being delivered to him personally.
When I walked out of the house I went to my office, and they told me they had been in touch with Regina. They had been told that when Mr. Thomson tried to locate Premier Douglas he found he was at a banquet. He took the letter to the banquet and as Mr. Douglas was engaged, I suppose in making a speech or doing something else, he gave the letter to Mr. Nollet, the minister of agriculture, and asked him to give the letter to Mr. Douglas as soon as he was not engaged. I assume, since there is a difference of two hours between our time and Regina time, that the letter was delivered at least to one member of the government before I had actually got to that part of my speech, which took some considerable time.
Two hours' difference; midnight, Ottawa time.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There is a difference of two hours in the opposite direction; my speech was forty minutes long, and this was the last thing I dealt with in my speech. Therefore, whether or not Mr. Douglas had read it, I think the letter was in the hands of the government before I undertook to place it on the record here. Whether or not it was, it was my intention that the letter should be left there to be delivered in order to make absolutely certain that it was in his hands by the time it was produced here in the house. I make no apologies for following that plan which was adopted at the time.
I have no criticism to make, either, of the fact that the leader of the C.C.F. party has placed the letters on the record. I have them here, and I was going to put them on the record some time before we got through with this discussion if someone else did not do so. There is only one letter which was not read into the record and I think I should read it as close to the time the other letters were read as it is possible for me to do so. It is rather lengthy, and is only reviewed in the letter which I read to the house the other evening. I replied to the letter of August 2 on August 15, and this is the statement I had prepared for the government at Regina. It reads as follows:
Supply-Agriculture
I have yours of August 2 and in reply would state that the government is experiencing a little difficulty in securing the services of the type of person they desire to have the opinion of as to what would likely be the result upon the Canadian economy of constructing a dam on the South Saskatchewan river. It was hoped that someone with sufficient standing could be secured as chairman to warrant that whatever recommendation is made would likely carry weight with the general public. I may state to you confidentially-
This is the reason the hon. member did not have the letter. The word "confidentially" is used in the letter to the premier, and I suppose he did not feel that he was justified in releasing it. But since the matter is now long past I do not think there is any reason for that, and I will read the letter just as it is.
I continue:
I may state to you confidentially that two persons have already been approached who, after some consideration, have decided that they could not find the time to take on the work.
That explains one of the remarks made by the leader of the C.C.F. party a few moments ago.
I am afraid that if information were given to the public with regard to the matter it might interfere with the setting up of the committee. However, the government succeeded in obtaining the consent of two of those who were asked to form a part of a committee of three, and I have been hoping daily that a suitable person would he found to fill the third position.
I can assure you that no time has been deliberately lost in getting this committee set up. Every effort has been made to secure the services of the type of person whose views would be acceptable to all interested parties. I feel certain that the committee will be announced very shortly.
The other question about which I have been somewhat concerned is the fact that the lands and resources, including water other than in navigable streams, have been turned over to the provinces. This being the case, we have taken for granted that if any one of the provinces were to transgress against the rights of another there would exist some right of action in the courts. We had thought to avoid any necessity of such difference arising by setting up the prairie water board. It was my understanding that it was hoped this board would find it possible to produce an agreement among the provinces as to what the division of water actually should be, and that this agreement would be put in such form as to leave no question before expenditures were made.
The question which you raise with regard to allocation of water for developments in Alberta would appear to me to be entirely outside the issue under discussion. The water rights which have been dealt with had been granted to the areas concerned prior to the turning over of the resources to the provinces. My understanding is that the whole question as to their right to the water has been settled many years ago. On the other hand, utilization of water on such projects as the Red Deer in Alberta and the South Saskatchewan in Saskatchewan has not been dealt with. If that is the case, it would be advisable to have a decision reached before an effort is made to obtain final decision at Ottawa.
I do not think that it is reasonable to suppose that Ottawa is going to put up a battle for the right to spend money in Saskatchewan. I would hope that the Saskatchewan government would feel that there was some obligation upon them to clear

S upply-A gricu Iture
up any differences which may exist between Saskatchewan and Alberta or Saskatchewan and Manitoba. I do not think that obligation should rest with the federal government, and I am afraid that unless it is borne by the Saskatchewan government there could be considerable delay in obtaining consent to the expenditure of money for any purpose upon or toward the development or utilization of waters of the Saskatchewan river.
What I am attempting to suggest is that in my opinion the province insisted on having the obligation to develop its own resources prior to 1931. They were finally given that right. It would appear to me that if they are suggesting now that the federal government should assume the cost in whole or in part of any undertaking to develop the resources they should first clear away any differences which may develop as between the provinces themselves which could result in damages being claimed against the party which undertakes to carry out the particular development.
This was the final letter in the group of letters, and it does deal directly with some of the questions raised by the leader of the C.C.F. party.

Does the minister not think it is an indication of their good faith and their intention to settle this water problem that they gave their consent to the St. Mary dam project and the allocation of water in that regard? Were they not prepared to clear up this matter of water rights at any time?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I hope nobody can quote anything I have said at any time which suggests bad faith on the part of the Saskatchewan government. I have never had any intention of doing so, and I am certainly not going to do so now. I would say that at any time I have been discussing the question with the Saskatchewan government, I have not gone quite so far as has been suggested in the reading of the letters which have been read; and in order to make it plain as to what the position is I think one only needs to read again the letter which I read to the house the other evening I gave a review of all these letters and the discussions which had taken place. The first discussion, which was referred to in the remarks of my hon. friend, was on June 24, 1950. The only reason I went to Regina to discuss the matter on that date was because of what I have just read from the letter that was not read previously, namely the fact that these resources were under the control of the provinces.
We had discussions on the floor of the house during which members had got up and said the province had nothing to do with this matter, that the province should have nothing to do with it, that this was a project which was entirely the idea of the federal government, and being entirely the idea of the federal government we should pay for everything having to do with it. In

order to make it perfectly plain that that kind of discussion would probably not get us very far, after we had been discussing the matter here I said in the house, without having communicated with the Saskatchewan government, as the hon. member has pointed out, that I was going to see the Saskatchewan government. I had my mind made up then to be in Regina on a certain day, and I said I would see them. It is true that wires came through before I had the arrangements made; nevertheless I was there and saw them, as I had announced to the house.
I went there for the purpose of clearing up something we had been discussing here, and to point out to the province that if anyone was legally obligated to do these jobs it was the province and not the dominion government. I pointed out that the fact that we were putting our engineers to work in order to develop possible projects was not any assurance to anyone that we were going to undertake the projects. We would make a report first to the province concerned as to what the possibilities were, and then we would discuss the matter with them under plans which we had already agreed upon and about which we had already passed an order in council. Those discussions would take place under those plans.
I made that known to the government of Saskatchewan on my first visit. I think we met them for about an hour in Mr. Fines' office. Mr. Douglas was not home at the time, and Mr. Fines acted as chairman of the meeting. All the other members of the government were there, and we made it as plain to them as we could that this was a matter which was still in the embryo stage, so to speak. It was one of those projects upon which we had put engineers, but about which we had announced no policy in connection with construction, and we wanted it understood that if there were an arrangement it would have to be agreed upon.
That was the August meeting in 1950?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It was June 24, 1950.

Subsequently, may I point
out to the minister, you came to a tentative understanding with regard to cost.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I know this story pretty
well by heart. You do not need to hurry me on it. I will get to it all right. The meeting of June 24 was a preliminary meeting before there were any reports in connection with the matter, at which we announced to them that there was a possibility of building a dam on the South Saskatchewan river at Coteau creek. We said the engineers had come to that conclusion and we wanted to

tell the provincial government that that was a possibility. Our reason for wanting to tell them was that, after all, the resources were under the control of the province. At the time it was suggested to us that the province was not very much interested in it.
Oh, well, it was.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Well, they did not say so.
Yes, but they were.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I was there at the meeting,
and you were not.
I was in the province.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
You may have been in the
province, but you were not at the meeting.
I understood why they felt that way about it. They still had the opinion that the federal government had been advocating the whole project, and therefore ought to build not only the dam but the whole project. I pointed out to them at that time that, no matter what their views on the subject might be, in all probability when we got down to discussing that feature of it the federal government would not be prepared to go that far.
The matter was left that way, and then in February, 1951 I again met the government. On that occasion the premier was there. There was considerable discussion at that meeting. It started out with the same contention as the one where we had left off at the previous meeting, namely the contention that the federal government had raised the whole question, had raised the hopes of the people in connection with it, and that being the case we should finance it. I took the position that there would not be any possibility of getting a plan of that kind even discussed; that we certainly would not go any farther than we had gone elsewhere. The question was raised as to whether that meant that, because we had built the dam on the St. Mary, or had undertaken to build the dam, we would also build any dam that had to be constructed on the South Saskatchewan river.
At that time I raised the question of power, and we discussed it for some considerable time. Eventually the premier said to me just what he said in the letter. He said the Saskatchewan government were of opinion that we should at least build and pay for the dam. He said they were quite prepared to undertake the construction of the power facilities, and the setting up of the irrigation plan. It was estimated at that time that one would cost some $8 million and the other about $25 million all told, $19 million for ditches and the distribution of water and the
Supply-Agriculture
remainder for the levelling of land. He said they were quite prepared to say then that they would do that. If you read the letter carefully, you will find that as Mr. Douglas goes through it he says at two different points that that was a matter which was to be the basis of discussion. He states exactly what he said to us, namely that we ought to pay the whole cost of the dam, and he maintains that.
But in finishing up the letter he also says that he understands I did state that this could quite properly be a basis for discussion.
I agree that I did say that to him, that this could quite properly be a basis for discussion.
I went farther than that. I said that I thought the best thing for him to do in order to put his position before the government was to write a letter and state what his position was. It was that letter which was read here today, and that was the position of the government of Saskatchewan. They said, we are prepared to pay $33 million for the distribution of water and for the setting up of the power facilities. We do that conditional upon the federal government spending $68 million to build the dam. I am not questioning that at all; that is what he said. What I am questioning is the assertion that I agreed to it.
The hon. member rather doubted that himself, because he said the only reason I must have agreed to it was that I did not answer the letter until June. It is quite apparent he has never been in a government. If he goes back over the files I have created in the many years I have been in the government, either out there or here, he will find there are many times when you cannot write an answer to a letter the day after you get it. After all, we have a government of 20 men. We have to discuss these questions. I cannot commit the government to an expenditure of $68 million by going out to Regina and sitting in a roam with a group of men who have nothing to do with running this government. That should be obvious to anyone.
The next letter which went forward acknowledging this letter was one which was sent after we had discussed the question here in the house, and after there had been a submission made to the government. The result of that submission to the government was the suggestion for the setting up of a commission to investigate the whole matter further. We intimated what government policy was with regard to it. Now, I am not going to discuss what happened under the commission. The commission sat and heard evidence. The commission reported, and that report was laid on the table of the

Supply-Agriculture
house. It has been discussed in the press and by individuals right across Canada.
I am going to say this. No matter what I think of the commission's report or what anyone else thinks about the commission's report, I am not going to admit that having the commission report did not do any good. If it did not do anything more, it created an interest in the whole matter in this country which is worth having, and that interest was stirred up from one end of the country to the other.
This is not a job that can be completed in a few months or in one season. It is a job that, whenever we do start, is going to take ten years to complete. I am suggesting, therefore, that the matter of a few months' delay at the beginning is not as important as some people would try to make believe it is. It is just as important to have the public interested, and I think the public is interested now. The suggestion is made as to what is the government's position. I am not going to read the letter again. I have said enough to indicate what our position is. I think if I read the last paragraph before the letter in my speech of Monday, April 27, it would be sufficient.
It is, therefore, important for me to state the present position of the project. After considering thoroughly the information compiled and the views expressed in the report of the Hogg commission as well as the comments on it by the Saskatchewan government, this government has decided that we should be prepared to review and continue our discussions with the government of Saskatchewan on the feasibility of the project as set up by P.F.R.A. and the willingness and ability of the provincial government to assume the costs of what we would consider provincial obligations.
In other words, we have just simply suggested that we are prepared to discuss the question with them further. What have we the right to discuss under the order in council which sets up this whole matter? The order in council P.C. 2298, drawn up on June 19, 1947 and agreed to by all three western provincial governments as well as our government, states this. I am not going to read the first paragraph. Everyone can get it and read it for himself. It is just the lead-off in the order in council. It then states:
The committee, therefore, on the recommendation of the Minister of Agriculture-
That is the committee of the privy council.
advise that Your Excellency may be pleased to approve the following principles to govern the policy of the dominion in respect to such projects:
That is large irrigation projects:
1. Before Canada undertakes the construction and operation of a project it will be necessary for the province in which the project is located to enter into an agreement:
(1)	to transfer any water rights required for the construction and operation of such project;

(2)	to make available to Canada any provincial crown, lands which may be required for dam site, reservoir or canal right of way purposes in connection with such project;
(3)	under which the water will be utilized by the province or some other authority or organization on the terms set out in such agreement.
This is the point at which we were in 1951 when the matter was referred to the commission. So what the government has actually done is this. It has gone back to that point and said to the province, "We are prepared now to discuss the question which we would have had to discuss with you had we gone ahead back in 1951."
The province of Saskatchewan did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I will read the letter to the hon. member. He read it a few moments ago. I will read him our answer to it.
Then I just want to say this with regard to that matter. The province of Saskatchewan is not in a position today-and they will not be in that position until the water board makes a decision-to transfer the water rights to us. That board was set up by the three provinces and ourselves, with authority to recommend in connection with it. We certainly would not proceed without a recommendation. As the leader of the C.C.F. party has said, the last time they met they decided not to make a recommendation.

Will you proceed if a
recommendation is made?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I will tell the hon. member in due course. He is getting ahead of me.

No; I like to ask
questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The hon. member is getting too anxious. It is obvious to anyone that before the province of Saskatchewan can turn over the water rights to us, they must have the water rights. So we have said that we have reached the stage now where that question ought to be settled, as to whether they are in a position to pass them over. As to No. 2, they have already agreed to it. There are 80,000 acres in the South Saskatchewan river valley and along the sides of it that are owned by the province of Saskatchewan; and they have said that they will make those 80,000 acres of land available to the dominion if the project is set up, without any cost to the dominion. They have agreed to No. 2 already and there is no necessity for their doing otherwise. As to No. 3, they have to make an agreement under which the water will be utilized by the province or some other authority or organization on the terms set out in such

agreement. In other words, three things must be done before we can even start to talk to the province about doing the job.
The last was implicit in the understanding.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It is not implicit in anything until an agreement is drawn up and signed.

It was stated by the
province.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It has not been stated at any time by both parties; it has been claimed by one and not agreed to by the other, in some instances. But the position is this under that clause:
(3) under which the water will be utilized by the province or some authority or organization on the terms set out in such agreement.
In other words we must have an agreement. What we have said to them in the letter which had been forwarded to them is: "We are prepared to sit down with you and discuss the first question-are we going to get the water rights, have you applied for them, when do you expect to get them-and we are even prepared to talk about that matter now; but we do not see how we can get anywhere with an agreement to go ahead with the job until you have the water rights and are prepared to hand them over to us."
Was that policy followed in Alberta with regard to the St. Mary dam? They went ahead with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That policy has been followed throughout, except for this-
It was not followed as far as the St. Mary dam is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I would ask the hon. member just to sit down. I have the floor at the moment and I will give him the answer.
At the time the St. Mary water project was under discussion, it was not a question of discussion as between the province of Saskatchewan and the province of Alberta or the province of Alberta and the province of British Columbia. It was a matter of discussion as between the United States and Canada. The international joint commission had intimated that we would have to start operations in Canada, in order to indicate our intention of using the water, if we wished to get a decision that this water belonged to us. So we had letters pass between Alberta and ourselves, and Alberta agreed that no matter what we decided to do in connection with that dam, they would apply whatever terms we had made as a result of our discussions with the international people; they would apply the same
.	Supply-Agriculture
terms to whatever they had done and paid for or we, on the other hand, would apply the terms to what we had done and paid for. The result of that is that the Alberta government had built and paid for the first storage outside the St. Mary dam and reservoir. After it was all over we adjusted that payment by accepting responsibility for it and paying for it.
I just say that in order to indicate that this matter involved international questions that are not involved at all in the other matter, and they had to be dealt with in the manner in which we dealt with international problems. But the fact is that it was made known at that time that these were questions which still had to be discussed and settled. Now we have renewed the discussion at just the point where we left it then, and have said to the province that we are prepared to come and discuss this question with them. The letter means that. The letter says that. It says it in two or three different places. I do not need to say anything more about it at this moment.
A few moments ago the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar read a telegram that was received from the premier of Saskatchewan. The Prime Minister has replied. I think I had better read the two communications so they will be together in the record. The one which has already been read is signed by Mr. T. C. Douglas.
I think I read only a paragraph.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I shall read it all and we will get it all on the record. The telegram reads as follows:
Regina, Sask.
Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent, Q.C.,
Prime Minister of Canada, Ottawa, Ont.
On January twenty-third nineteen fifty three I wrote you indicating Saskatchewan government prepared to enter into agreement re South Saskatchewan dam and willingness to pay share of the cost. In House of Commons February ninth you stated that you were not afraid of cost but that you were not convinced that this was the best use to be made of the water. You indicated that if you were convinced you were prepared to recommend project to parliament. I am in receipt of letter from Mr. Gardiner asking provincial government to submit proposal for construction South Saskatchewan dam. Before submitting proposal or discussing agreement essential that we have from you categorical assurance on two points, first that you are now convinced that South Saskatchewan river project represents best use that can be made of water available, and secondly that federal government prepared to proceed with this undertaking if government of Saskatchewan assumes fair share of costs.
T. C. Douglas

Supply-Agriculture
The Prime Minister sent this telegram in reply under date of Ottawa, April 29, 1953:
Honourable T. C. Douglas,
Premier of Saskatchewan,
Regina, Saskatchewan.
Your telegram of April 28 regarding South Saskatchewan project has been submitted to my colleagues. Present position of the federal government is fully set out in Mr. Gardiner's letter of April 24. It does not ask the provincial government to submit proposals but simply states that the federal government is prepared to consider a definite proposal from the provincial government for co-operation in the project on certain conditions and to have Mr. Gardiner discuss with you the terms of such a proposal. Before deciding whether and to what extent the federal government should participate we must know what would be involved and to what extent the provincial government is willing to accept those conditions.
Louis S. St. Laurent.
In other words, I repeat that we are just back to where we were. I may want to apologize to some people for the fact that we have taken some time to have a commission make the report they have made and say what they have said; but again I say that is not all bad. A great many things have been said by the commission that probably should have been said by someone, and it has created a great deal more interest in the project than we had before. But what is set out is that we are back at the point now where "we want the Minister of Agriculture to go", as the order in council provides, "to Regina or the premier to come to Ottawa and discuss the project", and get a full understanding as to where we are going from here, and get both sides committed on this question, which my hon. friend would like to argue are not committed because I did not answer a letter, or something. We will get committed by sitting down around a table, putting it down in black and white, signing it and saying, "We have an agreement."

May I point out to the
Minister of Agriculture that I cannot see that the Prime Minister's reply bears out the minister because the minister's letter says very definitely:	"The federal government is
prepared to consider a definite proposal from the provincial government for co-operation" and so on. The interpretation he places on that, or the telegram, is entirely different from the interpretation I would place upon this letter. Co-operation in reaching an understanding or agreement is an entirely different matter from a definite proposal from the provincial government.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Here is what he says:
Your telegram of April 28 regarding South Saskatchewan project has been submitted to my colleagues.

That is the whole government. The telegram goes on:
Present position of the federal government is fully set out in Mr. Gardiner's letter of April 24.
He says that, and he goes on to repeat:
It does not ask the provincial government to submit proposals . . .
There is in my letter a suggestion that we would be quite prepared to receive a proposal that the provincial government may have a desire-I would not say they should not-to go ahead with the project themselves, and might want to say to us what they think we ought to do. If they have any such proposal, we are quite prepared to listen to them; but then it goes on to say:
It does not ask the provincial government to submit proposals but simply states that the federal government is prepared to consider a definite proposal from the provincial government for cooperation in the project on certain conditions and to have Mr. Gardiner discuss with you the terms of such a proposal.
All we require from the provincial government is word that they would like to have me go to Regina some day-I hope it will be after the session closes-and sit down and discuss the matter with them and listen to what proposals they have to make. We have made only two up to the present. One of them is that they must have the water rights under their control before we can proceed to discuss any project. The second is that if they are going to discuss a project for the building of a dam in Saskatchewan that we can assist with, then our assistance is not to apply to the production of power, the reason being that-
They have agreed to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
No; according to your statement a few minutes ago they have not. The production of power involves more than just putting an $8 million development plant at the dam. If we were to do that alone we would be supplying the cheapest power there is in Canada to a province. Every other province in Canada would be insisting that we do something similar for them, and there would be no way of avoiding it, if we once started into a program of that kind. Therefore we wish to have a discussion with Saskatchewan as to just what position they want to take in relation to that whole program and have some agreement on it before we undertake to go ahead with the project.
Until we have had those discussions, and until we have had those agreements, there is no possibility of this government saying we are going to build a dam. But I am going to say this to you. Once these agreements are reached and we have agreed that all that kind of thing is provided for, this

policy cannot assume anything else but that we are prepared to go ahead in co-operation with the province in doing the job.
Will the minister answer one question? Will the government go ahead if an agreement is made for the power project?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That is what the agreement would mean; the agreement could not mean anything else but that the government is prepared to go ahead. When we sign an agreement we carry it out.
Would they go ahead with the project?

Is the government committed to that? Is the government committed provided a satisfactory agreement is reached with the Saskatchewan government? If that is done, are you prepared to spend up to the amount of money suggested by the royal commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: What do you mean by the royal commission? My hon. friends have argued, and so have I, that the royal commission was not very reasonable. They were talking about an expenditure over fifty years, not an expenditure over ten years. We have all said that, and the government of Saskatchewan has said that, and we have accepted the statement of the government of Saskatchewan that they think the project could be gone ahead with on the estimates that were made by the P.F.R.A. We say, "All right, we are prepared to sit down with you and discuss the revision of expenditures under those circumstances." We are also prepared, as I suggested in the last paragraph but one of my letter that I read the other night, to find out exactly what it will cost to build the dam, and there are real ways of doing that, some of which were discussed this afternoon. If we had to follow everything the hon. member for Lake Centre mentioned this afternoon we probably would not be able to do it, but there are things of that kind that can be done.

There are a lot of
loopholes.

The Prime Minister said the other night in reply to a question by my hon. friend that the government is not prepared to go ahead, without further information, to recommend to parliament the expenditure of the amounts estimated by the commission, and will not take upon itself to do that until it has further information.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
That is exactly what the letter says, and the letter suggests that we have ways of doing that.
