speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure that generally speaking throughout the province of Saskatchewan the announcement made by the Minister of Agriculture today will be received with feelings of widespread disappointment. The situation regarding the South Saskatchewan river dam and irrigation project is that everywhere public opinion has been aroused, and the people in general have been led to believe in successive general elections, as well as in the by-election in Rosthern in 1948, that there was nothing in the way of proceeding with the dam providing the engineers of P.F.R.A. came to the conclusion that the project was one necessary for the province, one that could be built and one that should be built.
The situation in 1945 as I remember it, and I am not going to give any quotations although I have them here, was that we in Saskatchewan believed that this project would be proceeded with. Following the election of 1945 there were engineering works carried out and expenditures were made from year to year to cover preliminary engineering examinations. By the time the 1949 election came along the Minister of Agriculture and those associated with him left no doubt in the minds of the people that this work was going to be proceeded with. Following that election the water board was set up providing for representation of the three prairie provinces. We were led to believe that providing the engineers of the government, acquainted as they are with conditions in Saskatchewan, would say this project would be an efficient and effective one, the work would be proceeded with. Then we were met with a royal commission, which postponed any action for a period of a year and a half.
In August of 1951 the Prime Minister spoke in Saskatoon and, according to the report in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix headed "LongTerm Value of Outlook Dam to Canada Primary Consideration..." he used these words:
The Outlook dam is a big undertaking. But none of us is scared of big things-if they are sound. We are not concerned with how we will pay for it. What we want to know is whether it is a good thing for the country.
Then he goes on to say-and I refer to the Prime Minister-
He was convinced that Canada would grow in population at least as fast in the future as in

Supply-Agriculture
the past and, in the light of this optimism, felt that such projects as Outlook and the St. Lawrence seaway should no more disturb this generation than the equally big plans for building transcontinental railroads disturbed Canadians of the last century.
Then he said this:
While the feasibility of the Outlook project had been demonstrated there was still some divergence of opinion as to its long-run economic merit from a national point of view and it was this question which the commission to be set up would study.
There was no concern then regarding division of responsibility as between federal authority and the provincial government. In fact, until 1951 there was never any suggestion that responsibility for any part of this project should rest on the provincial government. However, the question was mooted then for the first time by the minister, and immediately the government of Saskatchewan gave the assurance that this suggestion about provincial responsibilities in respect of irrigation would be accepted by the province. Only after that was the royal commission set up.'
As I look at the peregrinations in connection with this project it appears to me that at election time high hopes are raised. Between elections they recede by twists and dodges and meanderings here and there. I must say that I had high hopes after the vote in this house in February that the government would at least show its intention of going ahead with this work. I am disappointed that the Prime Minister is not here for, after all, regardless of what the Minister of Agriculture or any other minister may consider to be the merits of this project, the final responsibility as to whether or not it will be proceeded with must inevitably rest upon the Prime Minister and other members of the cabinet.
I think those of us in Saskatchewan have a right to ask from the Prime Minister something of a definite nature regarding this matter once and for all. Now something new has come around, and that is that the provincial government has not yet made a proposition or is asked to make a proposition. A proposition for what? The question of money and cost was never a consideration, at least so the Prime Minister said in 1951.
When the matter was discussed in the house in February we had the memorable scene of hon. members from Saskatchewan standing up one after the other and saying, "We believe in this; we are all for it; we are all firmly behind it" and then voting against it. Today we are in the position where something new has come up. I hold no brief for the government of the province of Saskatchewan, but I do say that certainly
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
in anything I have seen and in any correspondence I have read that government has been careful to accept its responsibilities and in no way raise a smokescreen to evade its responsibilities in so far as the production of power and the distribution of water for irrigation are concerned.
Why this latest twist? Between elections the possibility of the dam being built wanes; when elections are called the probability waxes strong. This latest development was to say the least unexpected. I had always believed that the minister was a strong devotee of the need of this dam being built, but over the last eight years we have witnessed that twisting and meandering and dodging back and forth with new and successive excuses, all of which have resulted in postponement and some of which apparently had that designed purpose.
But to me the latest is the most surprising of all. I did not think the government would be able to produce a new one. After all, there are only so many cards in the deck, but this time the Minister of Agriculture has been able to reshuffle the deck of excuses and produce a new joker. I want to hear the hon. member for Swift Current get up in the house and join with us in a demand for this, because he and those associated with us can do it.
Who is "us"?
They will have no opportunity this time of voting on the question. My hon. friend and those from Saskatchewan who are with him had that opportunity, but they did not vote.
That was not the question at all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: You asked me to repeat my interjection. I said that we were not that stupid. The Saskatchewan dam was not the question; it was a vote of want of confidence.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Did I say something I should apologize for?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: What did I say?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: A few words must be withdrawn.
He will have to take it back.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Does my hon. friend say that-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Does my hon. friend wish me to retract? He will have to give me an opportunity. When he brought in the vote of want of confidence early this session he brought it in in such terms that he forced us to vote against the Saskatchewan river project or support him in an attempt to defeat the government.
Oh, oh.
Don't overrate yourself.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member has
explained his position as against that which was stated by the hon. member for Lake Centre. The hon. member for Lake Centre may continue.

The hon. member may be a parliamentary assistant, but that does not give him any rights over other hon. members. I particularly made it clear that it was not a vote of want of confidence as was the case when the milk subsidy matter came before the house in 1946. I wanted this vote so we could make a united stand. Hon. members talked one way and voted in another. They have been trying to alibi themselves out of it ever since. It is obvious that the interruptions indicate that my hon. friends have reason to feel that they ought to start to explain.
The fact remains that as far as the appointment of the royal commission was concerned, that was evasive action. I have before me a report of the remarks of the hon. member for Kindersley when he spoke at the annual meeting of the Liberal association in Saskatoon on October 8. I read from the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix as follows:
During the discussion of resolutions, it was suggested from the floor that one dealing with the proposed South Saskatchewan river development scheme should be passed.
The chairman of the resolutions committee

J. E. McDermid-replied that the group felt it better not to have one.
Retiring president J. S. Woodward asked: "If we do, would we congratulate the government on the appointment of a royal commission to investigate the feasibility of the scheme?" "There are," he remarked, "some of our fellow Liberals who do not approve of the appointment".
Mr. Larson was asked for his views on the subject. The Kindersley M.P. replied-and these are his words-"The royal commission on the South Saskatchewan river project has a lot of eyewash mixed in with it. The project," he said, "has been investigated by both Canadian and American engineers and found feasible". "The federal agriculture minister," Mr. Larson added, "does not want it to become known as 'Jimmy Gardiner's white elephant'
The Liberal federation finally agreed to commend the government for the steps it already has taken towards construction of the dam and power project.

And at the same time urge that nothing be allowed to interfere with an immediate start on the work.
There are a couple of questions that I think can be asked at this time. The royal commission expended a great deal of money on its investigations. Sessional paper 170D of April 20, 1953, was an answer to the following question:
1.	Who were the counsel on the royal commission on the South Saskatchewan river project?
2.	How was the sum of $66,935.07, being expenditures for counsel as set out in sessional paper No. 170C of March 27th, 1953, distributed, and to whom?
The answer of the Prime Minister was as follows:
In the question to which sessional paper No. 170C of March 27th refers, the hon. member asked for information concerning
(a)	commissioners
(b)	counsel
(c)	staff
As there was no category in which expenses for professional other than legal advice could be placed, the term "counsel" was given a broader interpretation than usual and the figure of $66,935.07 includes fees and travel expenses for persons rendering professional advice as follows:-
Details of the fees paid to engineers and solicitors are given. In the case of the engineers, the fees paid to three of them were comparatively small. Among the larger amounts were the following: D. Hays, $9,112; Mannix Limited, $35,000; G. Haase, $3,963 and K. A. Buckley, $3,286.70. The total was $66,934.71, including travelling expenses of just under $10,000.
The latest explanation is that the government is waiting for the province of Saskatchewan. Surely the people of Saskatchewan do not have to wait for something so necessary to the future of that province, as well as of the country in general, because of some created or illusive difference of opinion between the provincial and federal governments. Certainly fairness demands that I say that in everything the provincial government has done in this matter-and I restrict it to this matter-I believe they have accepted their responsibility. In other words they are supposed to provide that portion of the total cost involved in the power and irrigation works. I see nowhere any equivocal statement in respect to that responsibility. If there is, I should like to have it pointed out.
On the other hand, raising this question at the present time in the form in which it is raised cannot but have the effect of affording another loophole and excuse for the government failing to face the problem directly now. If the dam is not to be built,

Supply-Agriculture
let us know. If it is to be built, give us that information. I ask the Minister of Agriculture but one simple question. Is he prepared, regardless of whether or not the cost estimated by the royal commission is correct, and if the Saskatchewan government is prepared to accept its proportionate responsibility to the degree indicated by the needs of irrigation and power, to assure us that this project has now been properly examined, found feasible and will be constructed? If we can have that assurance, then as far as I am concerned the matter is clear and commendation is due. If, however, it is to become merely a plaything through the raising of a succession of new and sometimes fantastic excuses for not facing the problem, then that is not good enough. Certainly no one expects the dominion to accept responsibility beyond what is federal responsibility. But if the water board, representative of the three provinces, is able to come to an agreement as to the diversion, disposal and distribution of the waters of the Saskatchewan river, and if the Saskatchewan government is prepared to accept its responsibility for that portion of the cost involved in the power and irrigation works, then surely the house and the country have the right to a definite answer.
On the other hand, we in Saskatchewan- and this is true without regard to political division-are very insistent with respect to the need of this work being proceeded with. We in Saskatchewan have assumed our share of responsibility in connection with projects elsewhere. Over and over again we have shown our support for such things as the St. Lawrence seaway, other waterways projects and any other meritorious project needed for our national development. I am not going to argue as to the need for the South Saskatchewan river project because the minister and I would see eye to eye on that, but there has never been anything for which the people have been more insistent in asking, as to which they want us to face the issue and deny ourselves the luxury of alibis, and for parliament through the government to let the people of Saskatchewan know once and for all whether or not this project will be proceeded with.
When the question was asked before the recess the minister indicated that the answer was in the affirmative; but in the last seconds before adjournment, when the leader of the C.C.F. party pointed out that this was a somewhat different attitude from what was taken in February, the minister said that the stand today is the same as in February. Certainly there was nothing in the nature of

a definite promise in what was said in February. The Prime Minister was asked whether or not, over and above the investigations by the royal commission appointed by the government, the project would be proceeded with.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is speaking of a different February.
I did not hear the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I think the February about which the leader of the C.C.F. party was talking was February, 1951, not last February.

In February, 1951 the situation was different. I took it that it was February, 1953. In any event, in February, 1953 I asked the Prime Minister a very simple question as to whether or not, if feasibility plus economic value were determined as a result of the further investigations and researches asked for by the government, the project would be proceeded with. The Prime Minister's attitude was simply a qualified affirmative answer subject, however, to eventualities that might arise in the future.
I am not going to labour the matter and argue it over and over again because we have done that in the past. We in Saskatchewan know what the need is. We know that this dam will provide a diversification of industry that hitherto we have not had. We know that it will guard a large portion of central Saskatchewan against the repeated effects of drought. We know that we need industry in Saskatchewan if we are to keep our population there. We have been led to believe by the investigations of P.F.R.A. engineers that the project is feasible.
Political consideration aside, in the event that the province of Saskatchewan, to whom a definite proposition should be submitted as I see it, accepts the categorical terms laid down by the federal government-apparently the federal government does not intend to accept any suggestions from the provincial government, for it has had that opportunity in the past and has not done so-what we want above everything else is that the Prime Minister shall give assurance that in fact this work will be proceeded with and not delayed, played around with and postponed until after the next election. We do not want it to become an election football in 1953 and then be put in mothballs until the next election in 1957 or 1958. All of us are agreed on the need. There is no division between the members of any of the political parties. We want this matter decided so it will no longer be something which is talked about at election time, promised at election time, and forgotten thereafter. We do not want it put in mothballs until an election in 1957.
It looks as though we are going to come back.

I am not talking about the government; I am talking about an election in 1957.
Having said that, subject to anything that may require an answer, I have made the last representation I am going to make on this subject because the facts are there, the statistics are available and the records are in P.F.R.A. All that is needed now is action to carry out what has been so often promised. We want implementation of the promises that have been made that the work will be done.

Mr. Chairman, every time we consider the agriculture estimates we seem to jump into a Saskatchewan political scramble. I should like to ask the minister one or two questions regarding the South Saskatchewan, if the Saskatchewan members do not object. The minister has stated that he will be prepared to discuss the proposal of the Saskatchewan government regarding the South Saskatchewan project just as soon as the matter of water rights has been decided by the prairie water board. The question I am interested in is this. Will the federal representatives on that board be prepared to vote in favour of an allocation of water for this project?
I ask this question because the last time this matter was before the water board on September 5, 1951, a motion was moved by Mr. Scammell, the Saskatchewan representative, asking that an allocation be made. When a vote was taken the rest of the board voted against it. The reasons they voted against it were mainly covered by two points. Mr. Ben Russell, the representative from Alberta, stated that he thought an investigation should first of all be made into the North Saskatchewan project. At that time he said he was taking that stand on his own and had not consulted the province of Alberta concerning it. It is true that at a later date apparently he was able to convince the Alberta government that an investigation into ihe merits of the North Saskatchewan project should be made first.
I know some members have stated in this house that that project has been investigated on several occasions. But what they must keep in mind is that great improvements in the surveys have been made by Mr. A. B. Cook of the P.F.R.A. engineering staff. Under his proposal it will be possible to reduce the length of the canals by approximately 100 miles. In view of that fact I think Mr. Ben Russell's suggestion is worthy of consideration, and at least some study should be given to the alternative proposal. The Manitoba representative and the federal representative voted against an allocation being made 68108-288J
Supply-Agriculture
* at that time on the ground that the board should wait until it had a report from the royal commission.
The question which comes to my mind is this. If those two representatives were not prepared to have that allocation made before the report of the royal commission, will they be any more likely to vote in favour of it after a report of this kind? It seems to me they would be less favourably disposed toward it after reading this report than they were before. However, no matter what stand the Alberta and federal governments took at that time, personally I feel that Saskatchewan has the right to use its share of the water in any way it likes. After all, they are entitled to a certain amount of water. If they are convinced that the best uses of that water can be made through the South Saskatchewan project, then they have every right to use it as they like. No other province should have the right to say to them, "You cannot use the water for this purpose; you have to use it for some other purpose." After all, it. is the people of Saskatchewan who will suffer if they do not make the very best use of the water.
I wonder if the Minister of Agriculture could tell us whether or not the federal representatives on the water board will now be willing to support an allocation of water for that project. I can assure the minister that we will do all we can to see that Alberta supports a reasonable allocation.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It is probably necessary to discuss the situation in relation to the board before one is in a position to give an answer to that question. The water board was set up in 1947, not in 1945 as was suggested a few moments ago. The order in council setting it up was passed at just about the same time as P.C. 2298, which I was quoting before the dinner hour. The board was set up as a result of the fact that the three prairie provinces set up a water board and notified Ottawa that they had done so. They indicated that they were going to determine the uses that could be made of water on the prairies. We wrote them thanking them for the information, and indicating that we were rather pleased that they had decided to undertake the control and management of western waters. Well, we received a reply to that, that they had no intention of doing any such thing and they were prepared to cancel the board and have another one established on which we would be represented.
As a result this present board was set up. We desired to give this board the authority to determine what the division of the water should be. The province of Manitoba took exception to that. At first the provinces of

Supply-Agriculture
Alberta and Saskatchewan agreed, but later Alberta agreed with Manitoba. The result was that we could not get any other agreement than that any one province could veto the wishes of the others in the matter of water rights. The position now is that you must have a unanimous decision before you can proceed on any decision reached. I do not want to go further into the details than to simply state that. It is a fact that when a matter comes before the board, one province can hold up a decision.
I agree that it is not necessary to have a water board. The water board was put there to make it possible for the three provinces and the federal government to get together and, by reaching an understanding or agreement, make it unnecessary for us to ever carry this question to the courts in order to get a decision. We thought the board could come to an agreement, and when that agreement was reached it would not be necessary to have any controversy about the matter.
What we are saying at the moment, and what we did say in the last letter which was read into the record this afternoon, is that we are not prepared to enter into a matter of controversy amongst the three western provinces as to what their water rights are. We think they should settle that question themselves, and we should not get into the .discussion at all, particularly when they are .asking us to spend mopey on projects in western Canada. All we say is, "You settle that question and we will be prepared to go ahead and discuss the utilization of that water." Until they have settled it, we are not entering into the discussion amongst the provinces.
Coming again to the board, the set-up of the board places Mr. Thomson of the P.F.R.A. as chairman. Then there is a representative from the department of resources here, and one from each of the provinces. Under the constitution of the board a decision amongst the provinces as to what ought to be done in relation to that question has to be unanimous. This government is not going to mix in a question as to what the rights of Saskatchewan are as against Alberta and Manitoba; but any agreement which they reach will certainly have the support of our representatives on that board.
That is the point on which I wanted clarification. There is no question of a federal representative vetoing an agreement that is reached?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to pursue this matter of the South Saskatchewan river dam at any great length.

I think probably everything that needs to be said has been said. The record has been put straight several times already on the matter; the record has been changed and put straight again. I therefore do not think we can gain anything much by further discussion at this time.
There is one observation I should like to make, though, and it is this. While the Minister of Agriculture may never have been in the army, he certainly has learned to play the old army game of "passing the buck" a little bit better than I have ever seen any old soldier play it in my experience in the army. It seems to me that is what has been happening, namely just a passing of the buck, with regard to the matter of who is responsible for going ahead with the construction of the South Saskatchewan river dam. I do not think we can decide that matter in the House of Commons. However, in the coming election I think the people of Saskatchewan will be able to do something about it. They know who has been making the promises before the last two or three elections in the province of Saskatchewan with regard to the South Saskatchewan river dam. I do not think their memories are so short that, when it comes to voting, they are not going to be able to make a decision as to where the responsibility lies. I think we can leave the matter with them; at least I am content to do so.
I now want to deal with some of the things the Minister of Agriculture said in his speech in opening his estimates. The Minister of Agriculture, both in that speech and in a speech which he made previously on agriculture, placed on Hansard a great many figures which indicated that agriculture in this country was in a fairly prosperous condition. As a matter of fact, if the figures placed on Hansard were reflected in cash in the pockets of the farmers in Canada, I am afraid that 85 per cent of them would be paying income tax instead of 10 or 15 per cent as at the present time. That is the proof as to whether or not the farmers are really prosperous. They are prosperous when they are in an income group which is paying income tax. I do not think there is in the Dominion of Canada any other economic group in which the percentage of those who pay income tax is as small as it is in the agricultural industry at the present time. Not only that; the Minister of Agriculture has held his present portfolio for some 15 years, I believe.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Eighteen years, to be exact.
And he will hold it for a long time yet.

That may be; that remains to be seen. But I am satisfied that at least the Minister of Agriculture is going to run in his constituency at the next election, and that is more than the hon. member who is speaking is going to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: And more than the hon. member for Melfort is going to do.

I want to point out something else. I have in my hand the brief presented to the government by the farmers' unions in western Canada, and here is what they say with respect to agriculture. May I say that I have not heard the Minister of Agriculture deny it. They state:
The fact is that the net average return on capital invested in the agricultural industry was -under 2 per cent over the 20-year period from 1931 to 1951.
The Minister of Agriculture has held the position he now has for 18 of those 20 years. Yet the average return on capital investment in agriculture over that period, according to this brief, is less than 2 per cent. I wonder if anyone in the house can indicate another major industry in this country in which the average return on the capital invested over a 20-year period is less than 2 per cent. The Canadian Pacific Railway, in presenting their case just recently to the board of transport commissioners, asked for a 6i per cent return on their capital investment. They think that is a fair return for the railways. I think probably agriculture is just as important as are the railways. If the railways are entitled to 6J per cent return on their capital, possibly agriculture is entitled to more than under 2 per cent.
When this government enter into a cost-plus contract for war materials, or when they enter into contracts with various industries in this country for the production of equipment that is necessary so that Canada may play her part in the protection of the freedom in this world, they guarantee to the industries in this country which are engaged in producing those goods not 2 per cent but 6 to 8 per cent. I think that, in bringing about permanent peace in the world, the production of agricultural products can probably play just as important a part as the production of armaments. Yet we give no such guarantee to those in agriculture with regard to the amounts which they have invested.
The other day the Minister of Agriculture placed on Hansard a great many figures, and I just want to read one statement he made. It has to do with eggs. As reported at page 4441 of Hansard he said:
The average farm price of eggs for the years 1950-52 was 43 cents per dozen . . .
Supply-Agriculture
I hope he goes on a farm platform and tries to tell the wives of the farmers in his own constituency or any other constituency in western Canada that they received an average price of 43 cents a dozen for eggs on the farm during the years 1950-52.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: If he does, they will throw the eggs at him.

The minister also said:
To date this year the average farm price has been 8 cents per dozen above 1952.
That would be 51 cents a dozen. That is not a fact. At least you would have an extremely hard time to convince the producers of eggs in western Canada-and I think also in eastern Canada-that they have received an average price on the farm of 51 cents per dozen for their eggs. That is an average price. The minister does not say it is for grade A eggs; he says it is the average price received by farmers. I am sure the hon. member for Glengarry knows that his farmers, even right here close to the markets, have not received an average price of 51 cents a dozen for their eggs. They just have not received prices of that kind. I think the Minister of Agriculture is doing a disservice to agriculture in this country when, by making such statements as that, he leaves the impression that agriculture is really prosperous. Of course we are better off than we were in the thirties.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: My hon. friend has used that term again. He is the only member in the committee who accuses me of having said that the farmers are prosperous. I did not use the word "prosperous" when speaking of the farmers. I indicated the other figure that was used by the hon. member a few moments ago, namely that only a small percentage of the farmers are making enough income to be able to pay income tax. I have said that the farmers are doing better now than they ever did in any other three-year period.
All right. We will take the minister's words. He says they are doing better.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I have not said they are prosperous. I have not said that at any time.

I hold in my hand something I do not use very often. It is the Searle Grain Company bulletin of April 22. They say this:
The dominion bureau of statistics has just issued their periodic estimate of the costs of living and production of prairie farmers. The present figure for western farmers is 216-6 compared with 100 in the base years 1935-39. This means that it costs farmers today 2 166 times as much on the average for the things they buy for their living and production as these same things cost them in 1935-39.

Then it goes on to say this proposed ceiling price of $2.05 under the wheat agreement means in 1935-39 dollars 94-6 cents a bushel. The price we have received for wheat in the past three years has been about $1.85 a bushel, and the cost of the goods that we have had to buy has varied from $2.06 to $2.25. In other words, in 1935-39 purchasing power we have received about 85 to 87 cents a bushel for our wheat over the last three years, and the minister says they are the most prosperous three years agriculture has ever known.
You can take a lot of other things. Take the minister's own figures with regard to cheese. Here is what the minister said in his statement with regard to cheese as reported at page 4442 of Hansard:
During the years 1943-45, cheese producers received an average price of $1.91 per hundred pounds; whereas in the years 1950-52 it was $2.37, an increase of 46 cents per hundred pounds.
But according to the minister's own figures a little farther on, the cost of production had doubled. Are the cheese producers better off as far as the dollars they have to spend are concerned? Were they better off in 1943-45 or were they better off in 1950-52, which the Minister of Agriculture says were the most prosperous years agriculture has ever had in the Dominion of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am still right, in spite of what you say.

You may take other products as well and you will get the same story. It is not enough to say that our total income this year is almost $2 billion. It is what you can buy with that $2 billion after you have received it that counts as far as the farmer is concerned, and believe me it will take a lot more than the figures which the Minister of Agriculture has placed on the record, or figures which he may give on the platform, to convince the farmers of this country that they have more dollars in their pockets at the present time than they ever had before, after they have paid their expenses. That is not a fact. The farmers engaged in agriculture today are back to the position they were in in 1939-
Rubbish.
-as far as the value-
That is not true.
-they can get for the dollars they have in their pockets to spend, and every farmer knows it.
Every farmer knows he's better off than he ever was.

Here is what the federation of agriculture, which represents the farmers of this country, had to say about it:
With this thought in mind we believe that the evolving of a more adequate and more permanent national agricultural policy is the challenge which now faces, not agriculture alone, but all governments and all economic groups and the Canadian people as a whole.
They do not say that we have no problems and that we are better off than we ever were. Here is what they say about the present trends. This is the Canadian Federation of Agriculture speaking in their annual presentation to the cabinet. They say:
The seriousness of the downward trend was clearly indicated by the Hon. Mr. Abbott, Minister of Finance, in the presentation of his recent budget, when he reported the preliminary figure for net farm income for 1952 to be $1,861 million, a decrease of 12 per cent from 1951. In contrast with this decrease, official figures show that during the same period, farm costs rose 4-8 per cent.
I ask the hon. member for Rosthern who knows the agricultural position in this country better, he or the Canadian Federation of Agriculture?
May I ask the hon. member a question?
They are speaking for the farmers.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
The hon. member can make his own speech after I am through.
You can't take it.
He will have an opportunity to do so then.
He won't, though.
You watch out.

What are the Canadian
Federation of Agriculture asking with regard to prices at the present time, with regard to the position which the farmers find themselves in as well as with regard to butter prices? Here is what they say on page 5 of their brief to the government:
With the cost of cream production increased by some 15 per cent since the present floor price of 58 cents lb. for butter was established in 1950, we urge that this floor price be now increased to 63 cents lb. and established for a two-year period.
The government are continuing the present 58-cent price for a further two years. I do not know what the result of that will be; I do know what the result was two years ago when the Canadian Federation of Agriculture asked for a floor price of 58 cents and the government decided in their wisdom that

53 cents was enough. I know that as a result of that floor the production of butter dropped that year to the point where we had to import about 10 million pounds of butter into an agricultural country which should be able to produce everything we can consume in this country and some for the rest of the world. That is the result when the government fails to establish reasonable floor prices.
At the beginning of this year the government dropped the floor price of pork from 26 cents to 23 cents a hundred pounds. I know the minister will say that we are going to reach a balanced position in Canada where we shall be able to consume all that we produce. We may even go farther than that, because there has been a great decrease in the breeding of sows in this country as a result of the drop in the floor price of pork. That means that we might go back to a position where we would be importing pork into Canada, because of the shortsighted policy of refusing to place reasonable floor prices under agricultural products.
Reasonable floor prices are a protection not only to the producer but to the consumer in this country, because a reasonable floor price means that the producer will continue to produce enough to satisfy the market so you will not get violent fluctuations in prices. When the government fail to set reasonable floor prices under agricultural products they have not the interest of either the producer or the consumer of this country at heart. There should be a floor price which will not necessarily encourage the producer to overproduce, but will at least give him an incentive to supply our own market. Personally I think they should have incentive enough to produce more than just enough to supply our own market.
We are living in the kind of world today where we cannot hope to sit back and take the selfish position where we are going to produce only enough for ourselves and forget about the rest of the world. We are spending over $2 billion on defence, and we are not spending one dollar in economic aid for every $100 that we are spending on defence. I heard on the radio just last night an address by Mr. Hugh Keenleyside, our representative at the United Nations, given before a United States audience, in which he said to them what he has said in Canada, namely that in this country we are not playing our fair part in the world today in combating communism, when we are sitting back and spending $100 for arms and spending only $1 for economic aid. The quickest way to provide more in the way of economic aid is to produce more food in this country. Surely we should have a government which is far-
Supply-Agriculture
sighted, which has the interests of freedom at heart, and which wishes to see a world in which we can have peace and plenty. If they have that interest at heart then I want to say that the surest way to achieve it is to see that agriculture in this country is given an opportunity to produce to capacity. That industry does not want to sit back at half production.
Produce for use, not for profit.
I would say yes, produce for use. I would say that we are only going to have the type of world in which we can have peace when we do produce for use.
That's not what you are doing now.

When the only incentive to produce is profit, people are selfish enough that they will take the profit and it does not matter to them what happens to the rest of the world. It does not matter what happens to their own neighbours. If that is the situation, then I say that you are not building a>
world in which we can have peace, and I am not afraid to go on any platform in Canada and say so. I have said it before in this house and I am going to say it again.
You are producing for profit now.

and provokes those who have been interrupting, he can expect to have further interruptions. The hon. member may continue, but he should speak about agriculture.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
I do say that our agricultural policy in this country during the last two years has not been one that has encouraged production.
It has made some of you socialists rich.

The Minister of Agriculture placed figures on Hansard in a speech some two weeks ago, when he compared certain periods of production in this country. I believe he compared the years 1943 to 1945 with the last three years. His figures showed that while the cash returns for farm products had been greater in practically every product such as bacon, eggs, milk and things in which the farmer can increase his production, yet the actual production during the first three years was greater than it was during the last three years. Grain was the only thing in which there was greater production. Surely, we have had bumper crops in the last three years; we have had a record production of grain, but I do not think even the Minister of Agriculture or this government can take credit for it or endeavour to take credit for it.
You would. Mr. Douglas takes credit for it.

We have just been fortunate to have had three years of high production in this country. As far as the things over which the farmer has control are concerned, production of those products has decreased and not increased during the last three years.
How much have you lost?

As I said before, we have not been encouraging the farmer to go out and produce to his maximum capacity. That is what the farmers prefer to do. They prefer to produce to the maximum and not curtail their production. They are not in the same position as the manufacturer.

As a peaceful member of the house who does not want to scratch his neighbours, I would just like to have a few moments to deal with a return that was tabled in my name some weeks ago. It had to do with subsidies paid to agriculture and the questions read as follows:
1.	During the past 13 years what subsidies and other aid have been paid to farmers?
2.	On what particular products were the subsidies paid and what amount on each, each year?
3.	During the same period what subsidies and other aids were paid to the gold mining industry?
There was quite a detailed answer brought down and, since the return has been tabled,

it has received fairly wide publicity throughout Canada. Because farmers seem to be living in such prosperous conditions-I said "seem to be" and I do not entirely agree, because some are better off and some are not better off-I have had a number of letters dealing with the matter. I find in the list of subsidies many things which should not be included. The total amount of the subsidies paid by the Department of Agriculture, the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation and the Canadian Sugar Stabilization Corporation is $1,017,625,000. That is everything that could be gathered up during the past 13 years. I learned a little subtraction and addition when I went to school, and I should like to do a little subtracting now.
I find in this list an item of $2,163,000 for the removal of apple trees. I presume that would be in Nova Scotia. There is another item covering compensation to seed dealers, $66,000. Then compensation for diseased animals slaughtered, $10,673,000. I assume that would be the amount paid on account of foot-and-mouth disease. Then feed, freight assistance, $180,746,000. Much of that would be paid to people who are feeders and not farmers. Then an item of $86,388,000 for wheat acreage reduction. That was paid to farmers during the war years to take their land out of wheat, to either summerfallow it or sow it to coarse grains. Replacement of maple production equipment, $2,249,000. That does not look to me like an agriculture subsidy. P.F.R.A., which is a government proposition, $32,261,000; maritime marshland rehabilitation, $2,845,000; drainage and land reclamation in the Lillooet valley, $704,000, and land reclamation and development in British Columbia, $1,462,000. Major irrigation and conservation projects in the prairie provinces, which I expect would take in the St. Mary river and Red Deer river projects, $21,435,000; flood control projects in Manitoba, which would be for the protection of city people as well as some on the land, $539,000; St. Mary river dam project, $2,339,000; cord wood, $2,098,000; milk subsidies, which was entirely a consumer subsidy, $76,598,000.
Those add up to a total of $422,566,000. When that is deducted from the original amount I gave of $1,017,625,000, we are left with a net total subsidy of $595,059,000. I could go into this in greater detail, but I do not think it is necessary. What I have given will perhaps help to dispel some of the false ideas held by some people throughout the country.
We have more than one million workers in agriculture at the present time, and during the years under review we had many more.

Mr. Chairman, I am not an agriculturist but I should like to deal with something closely akin to agriculture. I want to talk about Newfoundland dogs. One of the minor, or perhaps major, industries that we have in Newfoundland is the breeding of Newfoundland dogs. Many hon. members who know these dogs are aware that they are fine animals. However, because of a foolish regulation which the minister introduced during the last few years, the breeding of dogs in Newfoundland has practically stopped. As I understand it, this regulation requires that a dog be tattooed and nose-printed. The nose-printing of a puppy may be something the minister can do, but I do not think any ordinary person can do it. I was going to use stronger language.
I am not giving my own opinion; I am speaking from the knowledge of the chief breeder of Newfoundland dogs in Newfoundland. This man has bred these dogs for many years. He has shown dogs in various countries of the world, and has written a textbook on them. He has judged dogs in New York as well as up here. He has written to the minister about this matter and has talked with him. I think that should be sufficient to give the minister the picture I want to give him tonight.
I propose to read a letter which was written by this gentleman to the minister in June, 1952, a copy of which I believe the minister has. It demonstrates the point I wish to make much better than I could do it. A copy of this letter was sent to the minister's private secretary recently. The letter is dated June 4, 1952, and reads:
You may remember an interview you kindly gave me last summer when I told you of my troubles with nose-printing dogs and tattooing. You promised as soon as you returned to Ottawa you would have this untried impractical method of registration satisfactorily amended.
My reason for writing you now is to advise you that for some time I have been asked to reprint my little book on the Newfoundland dog. There have been some 10,000 copies sold and I purpose another addition of 3 or 4 thousand and I thought I might add a chapter on Canada's precipitating an untried, tedious nose-printing and an equally troublesome and impractical tattooing, neither of which is favoured in England and in the U.S.A. They ignore nose-prints and refuse to read lip-tattoos.
I again judged at the Westminster show, Madison Square Gardens this February and had occasion to hear the views of dog fanciers.

Supply-Agriculture
Although I deeply regret the trouble you are having with foot-and-mouth in cattle-
That was the time the minister was having a little trouble.
-I trust you will consider the personal trouble I am having with the new registry demands, which are sabotaging a very valuable Canadian industry.
I never register the Irish terriers as there is a fair demand (at lower price) as pets but there is a clamour in the States for all the Newfoundlands I can supply but I find that the Newfoundland's-
Meaning dogs, of course.
-nose sweats so quickly that a blotter or duster is
not sufficient to keep back the excessive moisture long enough to imprint anything other than a blur. After waiting a month, I received word from Ottawa that the prints were not acceptable and I secured Newfoundland's fingerprint expert-
That was the head constable of the police force, who was trained at Scotland Yard.
-and he tried three methods before he got what he considered indifferent prints though acceptable in Ottawa.
I am not alone in the dissatisfaction caused as three dog breeders of Newfoundlands of the five in this province have, or are closing their kennels and I have reduced my dogs from seven to three. Even if I get successful nose-prints in an all-black litter of Newfoundlands, it would be difficult to know which nose-print belongs to which dog. The five puppies I recently had registered were distinctively marked, one each sex all black and of the three male puppies, white on chest, white on right hind foot and the other left hind foot.
Regarding tattooing, many of the Newfoundlands have all black skin-
Again referring to dogs.
-and it is impossible to find tattoo marks and the whole scheme is frowned upon by U.K. and Q.S'.A. breeders.
I believe I read recently that some senator in the United States was objecting to Newfoundland becoming a part of the United States because a lot of the people were non-Caucasians. They are not actually. I continue:
After all, over 99 per cent of the dogs are pets and of the other 1 per cent how many would ever be lost or traced through nose prints?
Last year Maclean's wrote an article claiming that the dog industry in Canada was worth an annual $30 million. Isn't it a pity to jeopardize or curtail this through the whim of possibly a cattleman-
That is not the minister or his adviser.
-in the case of tattooing and an impractical crank in the case of nose prints?
It seems a pity for one who was presented with a sterling trophy by the Newfoundland club of America, engraved 1902-1952 for breeding Newfoundlands, and to whom a journalist in this month's Maclean's refers as "a St. John's businessman and the world's best breeder of Newfoundlands."
I readily could sell a hundred pups a summer to the States, yet two litters a summer with this new demand takes more of my time than ten heretofore. I cannot spare the time entailed as naturally some 500 employees, my family's interests and a number of directorates take precedence.

The man I am talking about is well known to the minister. He is the head of one of our biggest business firms, and his breeding of Newfoundlands is really a hobby. I say to the minister that it is a great shame. I am not going to read any more of the letter with the exception of the last paragraph, which is as follows:
My hobby is now a chore and the breed is well established in U.S.A. so I'll throw in the sponge along with other frustrated breeders and hope the government will realize that in addition to time wasted and expense incurred, feeding a litter of Newfoundlands with lusty appetites for an extra month costs more than is economical or attractive to the average breeder.
I am not going to delay the committee any longer. I think the industry of breeding Newfoundland dogs, and indeed all dogs, is very valuable to Canada. From what I have learned through talking with this particular man and also with hon. members of the house, the method of tattooing and noseprinting that the department requires is absolutely impractical. Is the minister going to change it, or are we going to lose the whole Canadian dog industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Perhaps I might be allowed to say a word on this matter, inasmuch as there probably will not be anyone else who will want to discuss the question. As has been suggested by the hon. member, I did visit the gentleman and I saw his dogs. I have an interest in what has been discussed, but I should like to point out that the registration of livestock is not handled directly by the Department of Agriculture. We make a grant of $18,000 toward the organization that carries on that work, but the livestock breeding associations carry on the registration of livestock. That applies to cattle, horses, hogs and all other breeds of livestock, and it also applies to dogs. The kennel club regulates the marking of dogs. They had a very lively discussion about it. Some representatives only want to have nose markings in the same way that you take thumbprints of people. They say that the noseprint of a dog is just as effective, and that it is the only way you can really distinguish one dog from another with certainty.
I do not know enough about the matter myself to know whether every dog's nose is different from every other dog's, but that is what they say. They say that if you take the imprint of a dog's nose you get the only sure marking. There are other people who want to have them tattooed. There are some who object to that because of the place where they are tattooed and the fact that it is particularly bad for a small dog. The tattoo sometimes gets too big for the dog.

I do not understand their reasons for all these things, but it is not the government that does it. I have suggested to those who have written in that they should get in touch with the kennel club so far as dogs are concerned, and see if they cannot influence the attitude of the kennel club. I should say that there is a set of regulations set up under the act with which we are supposed to agree or disagree, but I do not know just what we would do if we disagreed with their whole set of regulations. We have to agree on something, and we have agreed to tattooing and nose-marking. Either one or the other can be done, and that is the system that is pretty generally followed among kennel clubs.

While this country definitely recognizes that the government is going to the dogs, although not this variety, I should like to say to the minister that it is my understanding that the nose-printing is done under regulations passed by his department. Is that correct?

Mr. Chairman, I hope what I have to say will not be construed as meaning that I am in agreement with the hon. member for Melfort, but I do want to speak on farm prices briefly. I should like to draw to the attention of the minister a telegram I received from the county council of the county of Grey which reads as follows:
That whereas the drastic decline in prices of farm products has become alarming and dangerous for the future welfare of our whole Canadian economy, the county council requests our dominion government to take positive action immediately to correct this critical situation which, if allowed to continue, will force our economy to the depths of a serious depression.
The riding of Grey North which I represent is divided about equally as between rural and urban population. The urban centres, as is the case with most urban centres- the city of Owen Sound and the towns of Meaford and Thornbury-are sharing in the general prosperity of our country. There is full or almost full employment in those places, and the factories are operating at top capacity.
The farm community, however, is not so happy, dependent as it is for its prosperity chiefly on the marketing of hogs and of cattle. Grey county is second in the production of cattle and fourth in the raising of

Supply-Agriculture
swine in Ontario. As a consequence, since 1951 the Grey county farmer has been adversely hit by falling cattle and hog prices. While the national gross product showed a substantial increase last year, and while the national farm income was off only a little in 1952 compared with 1951, the income of the person engaged in mixed farming was decidedly lower in 1952.
This, of course, is contrary to the belief held by some city people, who think the farmer is making a killing today. There is no question but that the lot of the farmer is much better, and has improved tremendously during the last few years. I was interested in the figures given by the minister the other evening, which showed that farm products were selling at 2-5 times the figure they were a few years ago. I do not think the farmer would argue for a minute that he has not been getting a more proportionate share of the national pie than formerly; and mechanization, hydro and good roads have revolutionized life on the farm.
But life on the farm is still no bargain. In my county the proof of that fact is that the young people are still leaving the farms. The long hours on a seven day week basis, the risks of weather and markets, the shortage of labour and rising costs are the reasons young people are not staying on the farm.
As has been said so often, the farmer's real income depends not only upon farm prices but upon farm prices in relation to farm costs. As has been pointed out in this house many times, farm costs have been rising steadily, and in some cases sharply. It is difficult to estimate the rise in farm costs, because these costs vary so much from farm to farm. I noticed in the last issue of "The Farmers Guide" that the farmer's purchasing power, which takes cognizance of both what the farmer receives for his products and what he pays for his labour, material and other costs, if represented by the index of 100 for 1948 stands at 82 for 1952. This figure of 82 covers the whole field of agriculture. I submit that the purchasing index for the mixed farmer would be considerably lower than that. I do not for a moment subscribe to the statement that the purchasing power of the farmer is back to the 1939 level, as the hon. member for Melfort suggested, but I think it was lower in 1952 than in 1951. In other words, as my farmers say, there is nothing wrong with 20 cents for cattle as long as costs are brought in line.
Hear, hear.

I hear "hear, hear" from the opposition benches. I do not want to create
fMr. Bennett.]
the impression that the Grey county farmer is not appreciative of what the Minister of Agriculture has done for him. On many occasions the minister has said in this house that the best way the government can help the farmer is by fostering and maintaining a domestic climate in which there will be full employment and the resultant maximum purchasing power. This situation certainly obtains today. This government's immigration policy has also helped agriculture. As a result 800,000 new mouths to feed have arrived in this country since 1945.
My farmers also want to say thanks to this government for its support price program. Under this policy farm prices have been supported at levels which have prevented undue losses, and at the same time have allowed the principles of supply and demand to come into play. I think the farmers realize that if the support price is fixed at too high a level, production will be encouraged and huge surpluses will result. This has happened in connection with some products in the United States. If you fix prices at a high level, the only other alternative of course would be to control production. I think most farmers are individualists, and do not want too much government intervention, certainly not controlled production. In these days when we hear so much about hunger and want in the Asian countries, it is unthinkable that we should talk about controlled production.
Or limiting it.

Or limiting it, I agree. The government's action in supporting pork, beef and butter was particularly effective in Grey county because those, with apples, are our main farm products. In the last six or eight months many farmers have come to me without any prompting to state that if the government had not stepped in and supported hogs at 26 cents, the bottom would have simply fallen out of the market. I think this government has convinced the farmer that farm prices will never again be allowed to drop to disaster levels.
We all know that there is no easy solution to this problem of sagging beef prices. Even at today's prices the Canadian farmer is getting the best prices in the world for his beef. It is obvious that it would be difficult to support beef, either by means of a floor price program or with subsidies, unless the United States border were closed. I have heard no one suggest that such a drastic step be taken.
Some people believe we are now passing through the worst period so far as the price

45G7
of cattle is concerned, and that as soon as the cattle are on the grass the markets both here and in the United States will strengthen. I sincerely hope so. I am anxious to hear what the minister has to say about that. I recall that last year, when hogs were selling at 20 and 21 cents, he predicted that within three weeks the market would be 27 cents. His prediction was exactly correct.
The farmer is the first to admit what the minister stated on Monday night, that there almost had to be an adjustment of price in the cattle market. From 1946 to 1951 the price of beef rose swiftly and steadily, and without doubt some farmers made remarkable profits. These high prices, of course, encouraged production, and I think we are in about the same position this year in so far as cattle are concerned as we were with hogs last year. I know that in Grey county the cattle population has been steadily increasing in the last 18 months. For instance, on June 1, 1952, there were 148,600 cattle in the county, and six months later this figure had increased to 161,500. The farmer knows also that from 1946 to 1951 he was capitalizing on the fact that the Canadian dollar was selling at a discount in the United States. Today the opposite is true.
When the officers of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture met the cabinet last March, they said that if they were to pick one overriding thought out of the discussion during their convention, it would be that agriculture does not feel secure in its economic position. I believe that is the thinking which prompted the telegram sent by the Grey county council. The farmers are not particularly disgruntled. They are reasonable people. They know there must be ups and downs in the market in a free-enterprise society. They have confidence in this government, but this combination of falling beef prices and rising costs has them worried, together with the fear that agriculture, as a group, may be lagging behind the industrial sections of our country. The farmers want to be assured again by this government that in this period of our country's great growth and expansion the position of agriculture will be maintained as an important and basic pillar in our economy.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a
few words this evening about a problem which is of interest to the whole district of Three Rivers and more particularly to the farmers of Baie-du-Febvre, as well as those of five or six other parishes in the county of Nicolet. As a matter of fact, these farmers are now facing a most heartbreaking situation indeed.
Supply-Agriculture
Baie-du-Febvre probably has the highest milk production of any rural parish in the province of Quebec. One of the reasons for that is that it has the use of what we call the Baie-du-Febvre commune. This very fact explains why this village and the adjoining parishes have become the most important dairying centres in the province of Quebec.
The farmers of that district have always used this commune, which is already more than a century old, to graze their cattle, that is their steers, heifers and calves throughout the summer. This has allowed them to farm their lands which are among the richest in the province. Moreover this commune has enabled them to carry on the raising of really productive milch cows.
In summertime, there were up to 2,000 or 2,500 cattle in that commune. Lately their number has decreased but it has finally settled at 1,500. Most farmers of that area were using this commune for grazing their horses, and especially their cattle. That commune had a real importance in the area, for it helped increase milk production more than any other area in the province and Nicolet was the best agricultural county in the province.
Unfortunately, these advantages, these factors which are of such importance to the prosperity of the parish of Baie-du-Febvre and other parishes of the neighbourhood are about to vanish. That commune, which has contributed so much to the prosperity of the farmers, will soon be taken over by the Department of National Defence to serve as a firing range.
All Canadians and especially the farmers of our district want Canada to be well defended. They are ready to make sacrifices, like everyone else in the country, but they cannot understand why the Department of National Defence takes over the most productive lands in the province of Quebec to transform them into a firing range since there is so much waste land in the province that could be used for such exercises.
Anyone who has the faintest notion of the topography of the district could have explained that fact to the promoter of that famous national defence firing range. Unfortunately, the department, always desirous of clouding itself in an atmosphere of secrecy to hide something or other, sent its officers to Nicolet where they set up all sorts of installations, casting a veil of mystery over the district, so much so that today when people mention military works in Nicolet county everyone speaks of the Nicolet radar. Well, there has never been any radar in Nicolet and there probably never will be. It is only a firing range, where sailors or soldiers may hold firing exercises.

Supply-Agriculture
Had the Department of National Defence been frank about the matter and had it revealed its true intentions about this range, the local farmers, those who are truly interested in the local dairy production, would have lost no time in protesting against this seizure of the best farming land and might have convinced the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and his officers of the grievous injury being wrought by them on these farmers. In this way this famous range might have been moved further on, into the waste lands of the county of Nicolet, perhaps, but in any case, in such a way as to prevent this wastage of farming-land productivity in the very heart of the province of Quebec.
The province of Quebec has about 380 million acres, of which barely 28 million are fit for cultivation. Out of these 28 million, 10 million lie in the St. Lawrence river valley. It seems absolutely foolish for the Department of National Defence not to have managed to find, out of these 380 million acres, a bit of land suitable for range purposes.
Now, the study which is being made of the estimates of the Department of Agriculture indicates that this department intends to spend millions of dollars on reclamation schemes in order to transform arid lands into arable lands. However, all these efforts and the millions of dollars which are being spent on these projects will be wasted if the government, through its Department of National Defence, ruins the best lands in our province and causes considerable damage to the farmers of our district.
For these reasons, if it is not too late, I would ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to bring some of his influence to bear upon his colleague, the Minister of National Defence, so that, in the future, no more land-or as little as possible-be taken from this commune, even if the firing range cannot be transferred elsewhere. Moreover, I would ask him to see to it that the Department of National Defence, if it must expropriate lands, does not pick the best ones, thus destroying that which our farmers have taken centuries to establish.

Mr. Chairman, I have waited patiently all afternoon, and I have a few words I want to add to what

has been said already by various members throughout the chamber.
First of all, the minister's statement at the beginning of this debate provided a change of pace as compared with what we have heard in other years. The statement, while not an optimistic one, presented a fairly true picture except that the comparison of years was not exactly as it should have been. Then, too, statements issued by industry always give the net income. I notice that the Minister of Agriculture quoted gross income as far as the farmers were concerned, and ignored their costs.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It was the net income I gave on Monday night.

Everyone
knows that the costs, particularly this year, have been going up while the income from most products of the farm has been going down.
I am glad the hon. member for Grey North brought to the minister's attention some of the problems that farmers in that area are experiencing, and it is not confined to Grey North. Someone must have brought the minister up to date since he addressed some very optimistic remarks to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in Vancouver not too long ago.
Yesterday everyone in the house-and I am going to dwell on this for only a moment-was unanimous in the opinion that the international wheat agreement was a very desirable accomplishment. But in view of the fact that one of the chief importers, the United Kingdom, has not yet signed that agreement, so far as I am aware, it would seem to me that the agreement is another scrap of paper. Unless and until Britain does sign, the wheat producers of the world are going to find themselves in a very confused marketing situation.
In this as well as in some other policies the government have followed they have been influenced too much by opinion across the line. If it was not for the United States holding out for the price of $2.05 a bushel I think possibly we could have arrived at an agreement, and we all know that it would be certainly more desirable so far as Canada is concerned.
I for one have always been a bit critical of the government's apparent preference for dealing with the United States, and failing to cultivate and retain our United Kingdom markets as far as humanly possible with respect to trade. The desire of the western

producers to discuss the international wheat agreement yesterday was quite evident. They know very well they are not going to sell any great quantity of wheat to the United States.
I am one of those who believe that stronger and more effective measures should be taken to make the United States aware of the fact that we are not pleased with the embargo placed on dairy products, and we are not pleased with the prospects of higher tariffs. After all, we have some strategic and scarce materials that the United States must have. There is also the fact that the United States' supplies of raw materials are on the wane. That should be brought to their attention. They should be made aware of the fact that the good neighbour policy is something that can work both ways. While I am not suggesting that harsh measures should be taken, I think there is a method of approach that could be followed. We could point out to them that this can only add to the difficulties of two friendly nations.
The hon. member for Melfort pointed out that farmers were prepared to produce in abundance. I want to point out that farmers are being penalized because they have produced plenty. This government is sowing the seeds of another depression, first by its failure to grasp the opportunity to feed the hungry world; second, by inflation that has priced us out of world markets for our products, particularly our primary farm products, and also the action of the United States in keeping Canadian farm products out of United States markets by embargoes; and third, if we fall for the latest Soviet cold war moves. Loss of markets, inflation, overtaxation, all adding to the cost of production, are leading us right into the Soviet trap.
As a barometer of conditions on the farms, one need only go to the farm auction sales,

According to the Minister of Finance, in 1951, which was one of the best years as far as agriculture was concerned, 25 per cent of the people were engaged in agriculture in Canada; yet in that year they received only slightly over 11 per cent of the gross national income. When we come to 1952 we find that a lot of the people left the farms, and that in that year only 20 per cent of Canada's people were engaged in agriculture; and the trend is continuing. It is my firm opinion that the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce should take another serious look at Canada's markets for agricultural products. The results so far are not good enough.
May we call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
Item stands.
Progress reported.
